tiers.name: Foundations
tiers.summary: You can write and debug small Python and C programs, use the command line and Git, read binary and hex, and work out voltages, currents, power and battery life with the right units.

modules.title: Digital representation
modules.summary: Read and convert the binary and hex numbers, byte sizes and text codes that computers use.
refs: Bryant & O'Hallaron, CS:APP 3e, ch. 2 (Representing and Manipulating Information)
Harris & Harris, Digital Design and Computer Architecture RISC-V ed., ch. 1 (From Zero to One)

units.title: Bits and binary numbers
objectives: Explain why digital hardware stores information as bits with two states.
State the place value of each bit in an unsigned binary number as a power of two.
Convert unsigned binary numbers of up to 8 bits to decimal and back.
Identify the most and least significant bits of a binary number.
refs: CS50x 2026, Week 0 notes: Computer Science and Problem Solving
Harris & Harris, DDCA RISC-V ed., ch. 1

units.title: Powers of two
objectives: Recall the powers of two from 2^0 to 2^16, and 2^32 ≈ 4.3 billion.
Use 2^10 ≈ 10^3 to estimate 2^20, 2^30 and 2^40 as roughly a million, a billion and a trillion.
Compute how many distinct values n bits can represent (2^n) and the largest unsigned n-bit value (2^n − 1).
Find the minimum number of bits needed to represent N different values.
refs: CS50x 2026, Week 0 notes: Computer Science and Problem Solving

units.title: Hexadecimal
objectives: Convert between binary and hexadecimal by grouping bits into 4-bit nibbles.
Convert one- and two-byte hex values such as 0x3F and 0x1A2B to decimal.
Read the 0x prefix in code and #RRGGBB colour codes.
Explain why programmers write memory addresses and register values in hex.

units.title: Bytes, words, kB and KiB
objectives: Define a byte as 8 bits and a word as the processor's natural data size (16, 32 or 64 bits).
Distinguish decimal SI prefixes (1 kB = 1000 bytes) from binary IEC prefixes (1 KiB = 1024 bytes).
Convert memory sizes between bytes, KiB, MiB and GiB.
Explain why a drive sold as 256 GB shows up as about 238 GiB.
refs: NIST Reference on Constants, Units and Uncertainty: Prefixes for binary multiples

units.title: Text: ASCII, Unicode and UTF-8
objectives: Look up ASCII codes and use the patterns 'A' = 65, 'a' = 97 and '0' = 48.
Explain that Unicode gives every character a code point and UTF-8 stores each code point in 1–4 bytes.
Count the UTF-8 bytes for an ASCII letter, an accented letter such as é and an emoji.
Explain why a string's length in characters can differ from its length in bytes.
refs: The Unicode Standard, Core Specification, ch. 2 (General Structure)
RFC 3629 (UTF-8, a transformation format of ISO 10646)

units.title: Negative numbers: two's complement
objectives: Represent negative integers in 8-bit two's complement and read them back.
Negate a two's-complement number by inverting the bits and adding 1.
State the range of an n-bit signed integer, −2^(n−1) to 2^(n−1) − 1.
Explain overflow and wrap-around when an addition exceeds the range.
Sign-extend an 8-bit value to 16 bits.
refs: Harris & Harris, DDCA RISC-V ed., ch. 1

modules.title: Engineering numeracy
modules.summary: Do the everyday maths of engineering: powers, logarithms, unit prefixes, unit checks and graphs.
refs: OpenStax College Algebra 2e, ch. 1 (Prerequisites), ch. 3–4 (Functions; Linear Functions) and ch. 6 (Exponential and Logarithmic Functions)
OpenStax University Physics Vol. 1, ch. 1 (Units and Measurement)

units.title: Exponents and roots
objectives: Apply the product, quotient, power, zero and negative exponent rules.
Simplify expressions such as 10^3 × 10^−6 and (2^4)^2.
Evaluate square roots and fractional exponents such as 4^(1/2) and 8^(2/3).
refs: OpenStax College Algebra 2e, §1.2 Exponents and Scientific Notation
OpenStax College Algebra 2e, §1.3 Radicals and Rational Exponents

units.title: Scientific notation and SI prefixes
objectives: Write numbers in scientific notation and in engineering notation (exponents in steps of three).
Recall the SI prefixes pico, nano, micro, milli, kilo, mega, giga and tera with their symbols and powers of ten.
Convert prefixed quantities, for example 4.7 kΩ = 4700 Ω, 20 mA = 0.02 A and 250 µs = 0.25 ms.
Multiply and divide numbers written in scientific notation.
refs: OpenStax College Algebra 2e, §1.2 Exponents and Scientific Notation
OpenStax University Physics Vol. 1, §1.2 Units and Standards

units.title: Units and dimensional analysis
objectives: Name the SI base units (second, metre, kilogram, ampere, kelvin, mole, candela) and recognise derived units such as volt, watt, joule and hertz.
Convert units by multiplying by conversion factors equal to one.
Check whether an equation is dimensionally consistent.
Spot a unit error such as mixing milliamps with amps in one calculation.
refs: OpenStax University Physics Vol. 1, §1.2 Units and Standards
OpenStax University Physics Vol. 1, §1.3 Unit Conversion
OpenStax University Physics Vol. 1, §1.4 Dimensional Analysis

units.title: Logarithms
objectives: Convert between exponential form b^y = x and logarithmic form log_b(x) = y.
Evaluate log10, ln and log2 of simple values without a calculator, for example log2 1024 = 10.
Apply the product, quotient and power rules of logarithms and the change-of-base formula.
Use log2 to count how many bits are needed or how many halvings reach 1.

units.title: Ratios, percentages and decibels
objectives: Compute percent change and percent error.
Convert a power ratio to decibels with 10·log10 and an amplitude ratio with 20·log10.
Recall that +3 dB is about twice the power and +6 dB about twice the amplitude.
Explain why decibels make very large ranges of values manageable.
refs: OpenStax College Physics 2e, §17.3 Sound Intensity and Sound Level

units.title: Exponential growth, decay and estimation
objectives: Compute values after n doublings or halvings and model exponential growth and decay.
Explain the shape of e^(−t/τ) and what a time constant τ means (a preview of RC circuits).
Distinguish linear, quadratic and exponential growth from a table or graph.
Make an order-of-magnitude (Fermi) estimate and check whether an answer is plausible.
refs: OpenStax College Algebra 2e, §6.7 Exponential and Logarithmic Models
OpenStax University Physics Vol. 1, §1.5 Estimates and Fermi Calculations

units.title: Reading graphs and log scales
objectives: Read values, slope and intercept from a linear graph and interpret slope as a rate of change with units.
Use a graph to find where a function increases, decreases and peaks.
Read log-scale axes where each major gridline is a factor of ten.
Recognise that exponential data plot as a straight line on a semi-log graph.
refs: OpenStax College Algebra 2e, §3.1 Functions and Function Notation
OpenStax College Algebra 2e, §3.3 Rates of Change and Behavior of Graphs
OpenStax College Algebra 2e, §6.8 Fitting Exponential Models to Data

modules.title: Electricity basics
modules.summary: Calculate voltage, current, resistance, power and battery life for simple circuits.
refs: Scherz & Monk, Practical Electronics for Inventors 4e, ch. 2 (Theory), ch. 3 (Basic Electronic Components), ch. 7 (Hands-on Electronics)

practice.title: PhET Circuit Construction Kit: DC (build series and parallel circuits and check Ohm's law)

units.title: Charge, current and voltage
objectives: Define current as the rate of charge flow, 1 A = 1 C/s.
Define voltage as the energy per unit charge between two points, measured in volts.
Explain the water-pipe analogy for voltage and current and where it breaks down.
Explain ground as the 0 V reference and the difference between conventional current and electron flow.

units.title: Resistance and Ohm's law
objectives: State Ohm's law V = I·R and solve it for V, I or R.
Compute the current through a resistor for a given supply voltage.
Explain open circuits and short circuits and why a short can damage a supply.
Recognise parts that do not obey Ohm's law, such as LEDs and diodes.
refs: OpenStax University Physics Vol. 2, §9.4 Ohm's Law

units.title: Power and energy
objectives: Compute electrical power with P = V·I, P = I²·R and P = V²/R.
Distinguish power (watts) from energy (joules or watt-hours).
Compute a resistor's power dissipation and choose an adequate power rating.
Convert between joules and watt-hours (1 Wh = 3600 J).
refs: OpenStax University Physics Vol. 2, §9.5 Electrical Energy and Power

units.title: Series and parallel circuits
objectives: Compute the equivalent resistance of resistors in series (sum) and in parallel (reciprocal sum, or product over sum for two).
State that series parts carry the same current and parallel parts share the same voltage.
Find each resistor's voltage drop in a two-resistor series circuit.
Explain why household loads are wired in parallel.
refs: OpenStax University Physics Vol. 2, §10.2 Resistors in Series and Parallel

units.title: Batteries: capacity and runtime
objectives: Explain battery capacity in mAh and stored energy in Wh, and convert with Wh = mAh × V / 1000.
Estimate runtime as capacity divided by average current, with a safety margin.
Compare common cells: AA alkaline (1.5 V), CR2032 coin cell (3 V, about 225 mAh) and Li-ion (3.6–3.7 V nominal).
Explain internal resistance and why voltage sags under heavy load.
Predict what happens to voltage and capacity when cells are wired in series or in parallel.
refs: Scherz & Monk 4e, ch. 11 (Voltage Regulators and Power Supplies)

units.title: Breadboards, schematics and multimeters
objectives: Read a basic schematic with symbols for battery, resistor, LED, switch and ground.
Identify which breadboard holes are connected (rows and power rails).
Measure voltage across a part (in parallel) and current through it (in series) with a multimeter.
Explain why connecting an ammeter directly across a supply blows the meter's fuse.
refs: OpenStax University Physics Vol. 2, §10.4 Electrical Measuring Instruments

modules.title: Python I
modules.summary: Write small Python programs that make decisions, repeat work, use functions and handle files and errors.

practice.title: CS50P problem sets 0–6

units.title: Values, types and variables
objectives: Run a Python script and use print() and input().
Distinguish int, float, str and bool values and check a value's type with type().
Convert between types with int(), float() and str(), and explain why int("3.5") raises an error.
Format output with f-strings.
refs: The Python Tutorial, ch. 3 (An Informal Introduction to Python)

units.title: Operators and expressions
objectives: Evaluate arithmetic using +, −, *, /, // (floor division), % (modulo) and ** with correct precedence.
Use // and % to extract digits or wrap a counter around.
Explain why 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 is False and compare floats with a tolerance using math.isclose.
Explain that Python ints never overflow while floats have limited precision.
refs: CS50x 2026, Week 6 notes: Truncation and Floating Point Imprecision
The Python Tutorial, ch. 15 (Floating-Point Arithmetic: Issues and Limitations)

units.title: Conditionals and Boolean logic
objectives: Write if/elif/else chains and match statements.
Combine conditions with and, or and not and predict short-circuit evaluation.
Compare numbers and strings with ==, !=, < and >=, and explain = versus ==.
Predict the truthiness of 0, empty strings and empty lists.
refs: The Python Tutorial, ch. 4 (More Control Flow Tools)

units.title: Loops
objectives: Write while loops with a clear stopping condition.
Write for loops over range() and over sequences.
Use break and continue to control a loop.
Trace a loop by hand and spot off-by-one errors and infinite loops.
refs: The Python Tutorial, ch. 4 (More Control Flow Tools)

units.title: Functions and scope
objectives: Define functions with parameters, default values and return values.
Explain the difference between printing a value and returning it.
Distinguish local and global variables and predict which one a name refers to.
Organise a script with main() and the if __name__ == "__main__" idiom.
Add docstrings and type hints to a function.
refs: CS50P, Lecture 9 (Et Cetera): Global Variables; Type Hints; Docstrings
The Python Tutorial, ch. 4 (More Control Flow Tools)

units.title: Lists, dictionaries and other collections
objectives: Create, index, slice and modify lists, and loop over them with enumerate().
Use dictionaries for key-to-value lookups and loop over .items().
Choose between list, tuple, set and dict for a task.
Explain mutability and aliasing: why changing a list through one name changes it for every name.
Write simple list and dictionary comprehensions.
refs: CS50P, Lecture 9 (Et Cetera): set; List Comprehensions; Dictionary Comprehensions; enumerate

units.title: Files, modules and libraries
objectives: Read and write text files using with open(...) and the 'r', 'w' and 'a' modes.
Read and write CSV files with the csv module.
Import standard-library modules such as random, statistics, math and sys.
Read command-line arguments from sys.argv and exit with sys.exit().
refs: The Python Tutorial, ch. 7 (Input and Output)

units.title: Exceptions and simple tests
objectives: Read a traceback to find the failing line and the exception type.
Handle errors with try/except/else/finally and raise your own exceptions.
Distinguish syntax errors from runtime exceptions such as ValueError, KeyError, IndexError and ZeroDivisionError.
Write assert-based unit tests and run them with pytest.
refs: The Python Tutorial, ch. 8 (Errors and Exceptions)

modules.title: Python II and NumPy
modules.summary: Build your own Python classes and crunch arrays of numbers quickly with NumPy, then plot the results.
refs: NumPy User Guide: the absolute basics for beginners; NumPy fundamentals

practice.title: NumPy: the absolute basics for beginners (work through every example)
NumPy tutorials (start with the Moore's Law application: fit and plot real data)

units.title: Classes and objects
objectives: Define a class with __init__, attributes and methods, and create instances.
Distinguish a class from an instance and explain self.
Implement __str__ and an operator such as __add__ for a small Vector class.
Use inheritance to share behaviour between related classes.

units.title: NumPy arrays
objectives: Create arrays with np.array, np.zeros, np.ones, np.arange and np.linspace.
Read an array's shape, ndim, size and dtype.
Index and slice 1-D and 2-D arrays, including with Boolean masks.
Reshape arrays and explain row-major (C-order) layout in memory.
refs: NumPy User Guide: the absolute basics for beginners
NumPy User Guide: Array creation; Indexing on ndarrays

units.title: dtypes: float64, float32, int8 and friends
objectives: Name common dtypes (float64, float32, float16, int32, int8, uint8) and their sizes in bytes.
Compute an array's memory as size × itemsize, for example one million float32 values = 4 MB.
Predict wrap-around when uint8 values overflow, and convert with astype().
Explain why ML on small devices prefers float32 or int8 over float64.

units.title: Vectorization and ufuncs
objectives: Replace an element-by-element Python loop with an array expression.
Apply reductions such as sum, mean, max and argmax along a chosen axis.
Explain why vectorised code is faster (compiled loops over contiguous memory).
Time two implementations with timeit and compare them.
refs: NumPy User Guide: Universal functions (ufunc) basics
NumPy User Guide: the absolute basics for beginners (Basic array operations)

units.title: Broadcasting
objectives: State the broadcasting rules: compare shapes from the right; sizes must match or be 1.
Predict the result shape of combining arrays of shape (3, 1) and (4,).
Subtract each column's mean from a matrix using broadcasting.
Diagnose and fix a broadcasting shape error with reshape or np.newaxis.

units.title: Views, copies and matrix products
objectives: Predict whether a slice is a view or a copy, and whether changing it changes the original.
Use in-place operations to avoid allocating extra memory.
Compute dot and matrix products with @ and check that the inner dimensions match.
refs: NumPy User Guide: Copies and views

units.title: Plotting with Matplotlib
objectives: Plot a signal against time with labelled axes, units, a title and a legend.
Make scatter plots and histograms of measurement data.
Switch an axis to a log scale.
Save a figure to a PNG file.
refs: NumPy User Guide: the absolute basics for beginners (Plotting arrays with Matplotlib)

modules.title: Developer tooling
modules.summary: Work confidently in a terminal, manage Python environments, track code with Git and read error messages.
refs: MIT Missing Semester 2026: Introduction to the Shell; Command-line Environment; Debugging and Profiling; Version Control and Git; Packaging and Shipping Code
Pro Git 2e (git-scm.com), ch. 2 (Git Basics) and ch. 3 (Git Branching)
The Python Tutorial, ch. 12 (Virtual Environments and Packages)

practice.title: Missing Semester 2026: shell lecture exercises
Learn Git Branching (interactive branching, merging and rebasing levels)

units.title: The shell and the file system
objectives: Run commands with arguments and flags, and get help with man and --help.
Navigate with pwd, ls and cd using absolute and relative paths, ., .. and ~.
Create, copy, move and delete files and folders with mkdir, cp, mv and rm, knowing rm has no undo.
Read ls -l permission strings and make a script executable with chmod +x.
refs: MIT Missing Semester 2026: Course Overview + Introduction to the Shell

units.title: Pipes, redirection and text tools
objectives: Redirect standard output and standard error to files with >, >> and 2>.
Chain commands with pipes, for example grep | sort | uniq -c.
Search text with grep using simple regular expressions, and use head, tail and wc.
Write a short bash script with a shebang line and run it.
refs: MIT Missing Semester 2026: Course Overview + Introduction to the Shell (the shell language)
MIT Missing Semester 2026: Code Quality (regular expressions)

units.title: Environment variables, PATH and exit codes
objectives: Read and set environment variables with echo $VAR and export.
Explain how the shell finds programs through PATH, and locate one with which.
Use exit codes with $?, && and || to chain commands safely.
Stop a running program with Ctrl-C (SIGINT) or kill.

units.title: Python environments: venv and pip
objectives: Create and activate a virtual environment with python -m venv.
Install packages with pip and record them in requirements.txt.
Explain how per-project environments prevent dependency conflicts.
Read version specifiers (==, >=, ~=) and semantic versions (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH).
refs: MIT Missing Semester 2026: Packaging and Shipping Code (dependencies and environments)
The Python Tutorial, ch. 12 (Virtual Environments and Packages)

units.title: Git: commits and history
objectives: Initialise a repository, stage changes and commit them.
Inspect history and changes with git status, git log and git diff.
Explain Git's model: each commit is a snapshot that points to its parent.
Write a useful commit message and keep build outputs out of the repository with .gitignore.
refs: MIT Missing Semester 2026: Version Control and Git
MIT Missing Semester 2026: Beyond the Code (commit messages)

units.title: Git: branches, merges and remotes
objectives: Create and switch branches, and explain a branch and HEAD as movable pointers to commits.
Merge a branch and resolve a simple merge conflict.
Clone a repository and push, fetch and pull with a remote.
Explain when to merge and when to rebase.
refs: MIT Missing Semester 2026: Version Control and Git

units.title: Reading errors and debugging
objectives: Read an error message or traceback from the top and find the first real error.
Debug with print statements and logging, and step through code with a debugger (breakpoints, step, inspect).
Cut a failing program down to a minimal reproducible example.
refs: MIT Missing Semester 2026: Debugging and Profiling
MIT Missing Semester 2026: Beyond the Code (minimal reproducible examples)

modules.title: C I
modules.summary: Write, compile and debug small C programs that use integers, functions, arrays and strings.
refs: Kernighan & Ritchie, The C Programming Language 2e, ch. 1–4

practice.title: CS50x Problem Set 1 (Mario, Cash or Credit)
CS50x problem sets index (continue with Problem Set 2)

units.title: Your first C program: compile, link, run
objectives: Write, compile and run hello.c with gcc or clang.
Describe the build pipeline: preprocess, compile, assemble, link.
Explain what #include <stdio.h> does and what main's return value means.
Tell a compiler error from a warning, and turn on warnings with -Wall.
refs: CS50x 2026, Week 1 notes: Hello World; Header Files and CS50 Manual Pages

units.title: Types, sizeof and stdint.h
objectives: Declare char, int, long, float and double variables and print them with the right printf format codes.
Use sizeof to find type sizes and explain why the size of int depends on the platform.
Use fixed-width types such as uint8_t, int16_t and uint32_t and state their ranges.
Predict integer overflow and the surprises of mixing signed and unsigned values.
refs: CS50x 2026, Week 1 notes: Types; Format Codes

units.title: Operators and expressions in C
objectives: Use arithmetic, relational, logical, increment and assignment operators.
Explain integer division truncation and the sign of % with negative operands.
Apply operator precedence and add parentheses to make intent clear.
Use bitwise operators (&, |, ^, ~, <<, >>) to set, clear and test a bit in an unsigned value.

units.title: Control flow in C
objectives: Write if/else, switch, while, do-while and for statements.
Explain the = versus == bug and fall-through between switch cases.
Use break and continue inside loops.
Trace nested loops, for example printing a Mario pyramid.
refs: CS50x 2026, Week 1 notes: Conditionals; Loops and meow.c; Mario

units.title: Functions, prototypes and scope
objectives: Declare a prototype and define a function with typed parameters and a return type (or void).
Explain pass-by-value: the function receives copies of its arguments.
Split a program into two .c files and a header, compile them separately and link them.
Distinguish local, global, static and extern variables.
refs: K&R 2e, §4.3–4.6 (external variables, scope rules, header files, static variables)

units.title: Arrays
objectives: Declare, initialise and loop over fixed-size arrays.
Explain that C does not check array bounds and what an out-of-bounds write can corrupt.
Pass an array and its length to a function, and compute the length with sizeof(a) / sizeof(a[0]) where the array is defined.
Use a 2-D array to store a small image or matrix.

units.title: Strings, characters and command-line arguments
objectives: Explain a C string as a char array ending in the null terminator '\0', and why storage needs length + 1 bytes.
Use strlen, strcmp and strncpy from string.h, and explain why == does not compare string contents.
Convert and classify characters with ctype.h (toupper, isdigit) and ASCII arithmetic.
Read command-line arguments through argc and argv and return an exit status.
refs: CS50x 2026, Week 2 notes: Strings; String Length; Command-Line Arguments; Exit Status

units.title: The preprocessor: #define, include guards, #ifdef
objectives: Define constants and simple function-like macros, and explain why macro arguments need parentheses.
Write include guards for a header file.
Use #if and #ifdef for conditional compilation, such as debug-only code.
Prefer const variables and enums over macros where possible.

units.title: Debugging C programs
objectives: Decode common compiler errors such as implicit declaration, undeclared identifier and a missing semicolon.
Compile with -g and use gdb (break, run, next, step, print) to follow a bug.
Catch memory errors with -fsanitize=address,undefined and explain a segmentation fault.
refs: MIT Missing Semester 2026: Debugging and Profiling (debuggers; sanitizers)

tiers.name: Core engineering
tiers.summary: You understand how software meets hardware: memory and pointers in C, core data structures, small analog and digital circuits, how a RISC-V processor with caches runs code, number formats, and safe multithreading. You can estimate cost, timing and power at each of these layers.

modules.title: C II: memory
modules.summary: Control memory directly in C with pointers, structs, dynamic allocation and bit masks, and avoid undefined behaviour.
refs: Kernighan & Ritchie 2e, ch. 5 (Pointers and Arrays) and ch. 6 (Structures)
Bryant & O'Hallaron, CS:APP 3e, ch. 3 (§3.7–3.9) and ch. 9 (§9.9, §9.11)

practice.title: CS50x Problem Set 4 (Volume, Filter, Recover)

units.title: Pointers and addresses
objectives: Explain memory as numbered bytes and a pointer as a variable that holds an address.
Use & to take an address and * to dereference, and print addresses with %p.
Write swap(int *a, int *b) and explain why a pass-by-value swap fails.
Explain NULL and why dereferencing it crashes.

units.title: Pointer arithmetic and arrays
objectives: Explain that p + 1 advances by sizeof(*p) bytes, and compute the address of element i.
Relate a[i] to *(a + i) and explain how an array decays to a pointer when passed to a function.
Walk a string with a char pointer until the null terminator.
Read and write const-qualified pointers (const char *p versus char *const p).

units.title: Structs, unions and typedef
objectives: Define structs, access members with . and ->, and pass struct pointers to functions.
Compute a struct's size including padding, and reorder fields to shrink it.
Use a union to view the same bytes as different types, and state the portability caveats.
Use typedef and enum, and explain why C bit-fields are a poor fit for hardware register layouts.
refs: K&R 2e, §6.1–6.4 (structures, functions, arrays of and pointers to structures)

units.title: Memory layout: stack, heap and globals
objectives: Sketch a program's memory regions: code (text), initialised data, bss, heap and stack.
Explain stack frames, and why returning a pointer to a local variable is a bug.
Explain stack overflow from deep recursion or large local arrays, especially on small embedded stacks.
Decide whether a variable has automatic, static or dynamic storage.

units.title: Dynamic allocation: malloc and free
objectives: Allocate with malloc, calloc and realloc, and always check for NULL.
Free each allocation exactly once and explain leaks, double frees and use-after-free.
Find memory errors with Valgrind or AddressSanitizer.
Explain heap fragmentation and why many embedded projects ban malloc after start-up.
refs: CS:APP 3e, §9.11 Common Memory-Related Bugs in C Programs
CS50x 2026, Week 4 notes: Copying and malloc; Valgrind

units.title: Bit masks and bit manipulation
objectives: Set, clear, toggle and test bit n with |, & ~, ^ and & using (1u << n).
Extract and insert a multi-bit field with shifts and masks.
Explain why bit operations should use unsigned types and why shifting by the type's width or more is undefined.
Write a read-modify-write update that changes one field and leaves the rest of a word intact.
Use x & (x − 1) to test for a power of two.
refs: CS:APP 3e, §2.1 Information Storage (bit-level operations in C)

units.title: volatile and memory-mapped I/O
objectives: Explain what volatile tells the compiler and why hardware registers and interrupt-shared flags need it.
Access a register at a fixed address through a pointer such as *(volatile uint32_t *)0x40021000.
Predict how the optimiser can delete or hoist a polling loop when volatile is missing.
Explain what volatile does not give you: atomicity or ordering between cores.
refs: K&R 2e, Appendix A (Reference Manual: type qualifiers)

units.title: Function pointers and callbacks
objectives: Declare a function pointer and call through it.
Pass a comparison function to qsort.
Build a dispatch table (an array of function pointers) for commands or states.
Read complicated declarations such as int (*fp)(void *).

units.title: Undefined behaviour
objectives: Define undefined, unspecified and implementation-defined behaviour with an example of each.
List common undefined behaviour in C: signed overflow, out-of-bounds access, null dereference, uninitialised reads, strict-aliasing violations and over-wide shifts.
Explain how an optimiser can legally remove a signed-overflow check.
Catch undefined behaviour with -Wall -Wextra and -fsanitize=undefined.
refs: Regehr, 'A Guide to Undefined Behavior in C and C++' (blog series, 2010)

modules.title: Data structures and algorithms
modules.summary: Pick and build the right data structure and algorithm, and estimate how its cost grows with input size.
refs: Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest & Stein, Introduction to Algorithms (CLRS) 4e, ch. 2–3, 6–8, 10–13, 16, 20

practice.title: CS50x Speller: build a fast hash-table spell checker in C

units.title: Measuring cost: Big-O
objectives: Define O, Ω and Θ informally and rank growth rates: 1, log n, n, n log n, n², 2^n.
Derive the Big-O of simple and nested loops from code.
Estimate runtime from an operation count and a clock rate, for example 10^6 operations at 100 MHz.
Explain why constant factors and small n matter on microcontrollers.

units.title: Arrays versus linked lists
objectives: Implement a singly linked list in C: insert at the head, traverse and delete a node.
Compare arrays and linked lists on access time, insertion cost and memory overhead.
Explain cache locality and why contiguous arrays usually win on real hardware.
Implement a growable array that doubles its capacity and explain amortised O(1) append.
refs: CS50x 2026, Week 5 notes: Arrays; Linked Lists

units.title: Stacks, queues and ring buffers
objectives: Implement a stack and use it to check balanced brackets.
Implement a fixed-size ring buffer (circular FIFO) with head and tail indices, and handle the full and empty cases.
Use a power-of-two buffer size so indices wrap with a bit mask.

Use a Wheatstone bridge and an instrumentation amplifier for small signals such as strain gauges.

Weigh noise reduction against added delay when choosing a filter.

objectives: Explain what MEMS accelerometers (specific force, including gravity), gyroscopes (angular rate) and magnetometers measure.
Convert raw IMU readings to g and degrees per second from the full-scale range.
Compute tilt from an accelerometer, integrate gyro rate into angle and explain drift.
Fuse accelerometer and gyro with a complementary filter, and configure the output data rate, FIFO and data-ready interrupt.

Compute frame and hop sizes and buffer memory for 16 kHz audio features, for example 30 ms windows with a 20 ms hop.
Remove DC offset and set gain so loud speech does not clip.

units.title: Cameras and image signal processing

modules.title: RTOS

Valvano, Vol. 3 (Real-Time Operating Systems for ARM Cortex-M), ch. 3–5

RTOS sensor project, step 2: read an MPU6050 IMU over I2C (start from this sample and add a devicetree overlay for your board)

RTOS sensor project, FreeRTOS variant: build the same pipeline starting from the FreeRTOS Kernel Quick Start Guide
FreeRTOS Kernel Book and its examples (tasks, queues, mutexes, interrupts)

units.title: Why an RTOS: super-loop versus scheduler
objectives: Contrast super-loop, cooperative and preemptive designs on responsiveness and complexity.
Define hard and soft real-time, deadline and determinism.

Decide when bare-metal firmware is enough.

Arm Education, Get Practical with Hardware (Introductory Real-Time Operating Systems)

units.title: Tasks, stacks and task states
objectives: Create tasks with xTaskCreate (or Zephyr K_THREAD_DEFINE), giving the entry function, stack size and priority.
Trace the Running, Ready, Blocked and Suspended states and the events that move a task between them.
Size a task stack and check it with the stack high-water mark.
Use vTaskDelayUntil rather than vTaskDelay for a drift-free periodic task, and explain the idle task.

units.title: Priority-preemptive scheduling and the context switch
objectives: Predict which task runs under fixed-priority preemptive scheduling, with and without time slicing.
Explain the tick interrupt and the trade-offs of tick rates such as 1 kHz versus 100 Hz.
Explain how a Cortex-M context switch works with PendSV, the PSP and the stacked registers.
Configure preemption and time slicing (configUSE_PREEMPTION, configUSE_TIME_SLICING) or Zephyr cooperative versus preemptible priorities.
refs: FreeRTOS Kernel Book, §4.6 Time Measurement and the Tick Interrupt; §4.12 Scheduling Algorithms
Yiu, Cortex-M3/M4 3e, ch. 10 OS Support Features (§10.2–10.5)

units.title: Queues and message passing
objectives: Create a queue and send and receive with timeouts (xQueueSend and xQueueReceive, or k_msgq_put and k_msgq_get).
Contrast queuing by copy with queuing pointers, including who owns the buffer.
Build a producer-to-consumer pipeline: sensor task, processing task, output task.
Size a queue from production rate, consumption rate and burst length, and wait on several sources with queue sets or k_poll.

Zephyr docs: Kernel Services > Message Queues; FIFOs; Polling API

units.title: From interrupts to tasks: semaphores and notifications

Defer interrupt work to a task with a binary semaphore or a direct task notification.

Count events with a counting semaphore, and defer work with Zephyr workqueues.

FreeRTOS Kernel Book, ch. 10 Task Notifications
Zephyr docs: Kernel Services > Interrupts; Workqueue Threads; Semaphores

units.title: Mutexes, priority inversion and inheritance

Draw a three-task timeline that shows unbounded priority inversion, and relate it to the 1997 Mars Pathfinder resets.

Avoid deadlock with lock ordering and timeouts, or use a gatekeeper task instead of a lock.

Lee & Seshia 2e, ch. 12 (Scheduling: priority inversion and inheritance)

Wait for combinations of conditions with event groups (or Zephyr events).
Choose a FreeRTOS heap scheme (heap_1 to heap_5) or static allocation, or Zephyr memory slabs, for deterministic memory use.
Monitor free heap and minimum-ever free heap.
refs: FreeRTOS Kernel Book, ch. 3 Heap Memory Management
FreeRTOS Kernel Book, ch. 6 Software Timer Management
FreeRTOS Kernel Book, ch. 9 Event Groups
Zephyr docs: Kernel Services > Timers; Events; Memory Management

units.title: Schedulability: rate-monotonic analysis and WCET

Assign rate-monotonic priorities and test a task set against the Liu–Layland bound U ≤ n(2^(1/n) − 1), which falls toward about 69 %.
Run response-time analysis R = C + Σ ⌈R / Tj⌉ · Cj for a three-task set.
Explain how WCET is measured (cycle counter, trace) or bounded statically, why caches and interrupts complicate it, and how earliest-deadline-first differs.

units.title: Zephyr: devicetree, Kconfig and the device model
objectives: Read a devicetree node (compatible, reg, interrupts, status) and write a board overlay that enables an I2C sensor.
Get a device handle in C with DEVICE_DT_GET and DT_NODELABEL, and check device_is_ready().
Enable features with Kconfig options in prj.conf (for example CONFIG_I2C=y and CONFIG_SENSOR=y), and explain devicetree versus Kconfig.
Build and flash an application with west for a chosen board.

units.title: Debugging RTOS applications: the sensor-pipeline capstone
objectives: Catch stack overflows and allocation failures with configASSERT, the stack-overflow hook and the malloc-failed hook.
Use run-time statistics and a trace tool to find CPU hogs and priority mistakes.
Build the capstone: one task reads an IMU over I2C, another processes the samples and a third streams them over UART, with a mutex on the bus and a fixed sample period.
Measure sample-period jitter on hardware with a timing pin.

Zephyr docs: MPU6050 motion tracking device sample; UART echo sample

Choose a platform for a battery wake-word sensor, a smart camera and a robot controller.
Explain hybrid designs that pair a Linux application core with a real-time MCU core.

units.title: The Linux boot process

Read and change U-Boot environment variables and the kernel command line.
Measure boot time and name ways to shorten it.

Simmonds & Vasquez, MELP 3e, ch. 13 (Starting Up – The init Program)

Contrast kernel drivers with user-space access through /dev, sysfs, i2c-dev, spidev and libgpiod.
Read a GPIO and an I2C sensor from user space in Python or C.
Load and inspect kernel modules (modprobe, lsmod) and read driver messages with dmesg.

Simmonds & Vasquez, MELP 3e, ch. 3 (All about Bootloaders: device trees)

Build a minimal image with Buildroot (defconfig, make menuconfig) and with Yocto (layers, recipes, bitbake, MACHINE).
Compare Buildroot and Yocto on learning curve, flexibility, package management and build time.
Add a custom application as a Buildroot package or a Yocto recipe.

Simmonds & Vasquez, MELP 3e, ch. 6 (Selecting a Build System)

Debug a program on the target from the host with gdbserver.
Run an application as a service with a systemd unit.
Explain read-only root file systems and A/B image updates.

Simmonds & Vasquez, MELP 3e, ch. 19 (Debugging with GDB)

units.title: Edge SoCs: CPU, GPU, DSP and NPU
objectives: Describe a heterogeneous SoC: big.LITTLE CPU clusters, GPU, DSP, NPU, ISP and video codecs sharing DRAM and caches.
Explain why NPUs are efficient at int8 tensor maths: MAC arrays, local SRAM and less data movement.
Compare accelerators by TOPS, TOPS per watt and memory bandwidth, and explain why peak TOPS alone misleads.
Explain shared (unified) versus dedicated memory and the cost of copying tensors between accelerators.

units.title: Raspberry Pi and NVIDIA Jetson
objectives: Compare a Raspberry Pi 5 (quad Cortex-A76, VideoCore GPU, optional AI accelerator board) with a Jetson Orin Nano (Arm CPU plus an Ampere GPU with CUDA and Tensor Cores) on compute, power and software stack.
Explain JetPack and CUDA on Jetson versus Raspberry Pi OS on the Pi.
Switch Jetson power modes with nvpmodel and read utilisation and power with tegrastats.
Pick a board for a camera inference project within a power budget.

units.title: Real-time behaviour and profiling on Linux
objectives: Explain why a stock Linux kernel shows latency spikes and what PREEMPT_RT, SCHED_FIFO and CPU isolation change.
Measure scheduling latency with cyclictest.
Profile CPU use with perf and top, and check the CPU frequency governor.
Decide when hard real-time work should move to an MCU co-processor.

modules.title: Low-power design
modules.summary: Make a battery-powered device last by budgeting, reducing and measuring its power use.

FreeRTOS Kernel Book, ch. 11 (Low Power Support)

units.title: Where the power goes
objectives: Break a device's consumption into MCU active, MCU sleep, radio, sensors, regulator quiescent current and leakage.
Recall typical magnitudes: MCU active current in tens of µA per MHz, deep sleep in µA, a BLE radio in mA and Wi-Fi in tens to hundreds of mA.
Build a simple power-budget table for a sensor node and find the dominant consumer.
refs: Warden & Situnayake, TinyML, ch. 16 (Optimizing Energy Usage: Developing Intuition; Typical Component Power Usage)
White, Making Embedded Systems 2e, ch. 13 (Reducing Power Consumption)

units.title: Sleep modes and wake-up
objectives: Compare sleep, deep-sleep (stop) and standby (shutdown) modes: what is clock-gated, what is powered off, what is retained and how long wake-up takes.
Enter sleep with WFI or WFE and use Sleep-on-Exit for interrupt-driven designs.
Configure wake-up sources such as an RTC alarm, a GPIO edge or a wake-up timer.
Re-initialise clocks and peripherals correctly after waking from deep sleep.

Yiu, Cortex-M3/M4 3e, §9.3 Using WFI and WFE instructions in programming
White, Making Embedded Systems 2e, ch. 13 (Reducing Power Consumption)

objectives: Compute average current I_avg = (I_active·t_active + I_sleep·t_sleep) / T for a periodic device.
Find the duty cycle at which sleep current starts to dominate the average.
Batch sensor reads and radio transmissions to reduce wake-ups.
Use a cascade in which a cheap always-on detector wakes an expensive model only when needed.
refs: Warden & Situnayake, TinyML, ch. 16 (Improving Power Usage: duty cycling; cascading design)
White, Making Embedded Systems 2e, ch. 13 (Reducing Power Consumption)

units.title: Clock scaling and DVFS
objectives: Use P_dyn = α·C·V²·f to show why lowering voltage saves more than lowering frequency alone.
Explain DVFS operating points and why energy per operation, not power, is the right metric.
Decide between racing to sleep at full speed and running slowly at a lower voltage.
Gate the clocks of unused peripherals.
refs: Harris & Harris, DDCA RISC-V ed., ch. 1 (From Zero to One: power consumption)
White, Making Embedded Systems 2e, ch. 13 (Reducing Power Consumption)

units.title: Battery-life math
objectives: Estimate battery life as usable capacity divided by average current, derated for temperature, cut-off voltage and self-discharge.
Carry energy through a regulator: convert mAh to Wh and apply the regulator's efficiency (LDO versus buck).
Size a coin cell or Li-ion pack for a one-year target.
Check peak-current limits, for example a coin cell's internal resistance during a radio burst.
refs: White, Making Embedded Systems 2e, ch. 13 (Reducing Power Consumption)
Scherz & Monk 4e, ch. 3 (Basic Electronic Components) and ch. 11 (Voltage Regulators and Power Supplies)

units.title: Measuring power
objectives: Measure current with a shunt resistor and amplifier, a power profiler or a source-measure unit, and explain why a handheld multimeter misses short pulses (burden voltage, slow sampling).
Integrate a current trace to get the charge and energy per event, such as per inference.
Find sleep-current leaks: floating pins, peripherals left on, an attached debug probe.
Estimate energy per inference from measured current and latency.
refs: Warden & Situnayake, TinyML, ch. 16 (Measuring Real Power Usage; Estimating Power Usage for a Model)
White, Making Embedded Systems 2e, ch. 13 (Reducing Power Consumption)

Enable FreeRTOS tickless idle (configUSE_TICKLESS_IDLE, portSUPPRESS_TICKS_AND_SLEEP) or Zephyr's idle and power management.
Use the idle hook and pre- and post-sleep processing to gate clocks.
Compute the energy saved by removing 1 kHz tick wake-ups.

Zephyr docs: Kernel Services > Scheduling (CPU Idling)

units.title: Firmware patterns for low power

Weigh always-on detection against periodic wake-ups for a wake-word device.

Time code sections and ISR latency by toggling a spare GPIO, sampling at 4–10 times the signal rate.

objectives: Add and scale vectors, and explain both operations as arrows and as NumPy array operations.
Compute a dot product by hand and state that two length-n vectors cost n multiply-accumulates (MACs).
Compute the angle and cosine similarity between two vectors from their dot product and lengths.
Explain why a neuron's weighted sum is a dot product between a weight vector and an input vector.

units.title: Matrices and the cost of matrix multiply
objectives: Multiply matrices with the row-times-column rule and state the shape rule (M×K)·(K×N) → M×N.

Interpret Ax as a weighted combination of the columns of A.
State that matrix multiplication is associative but not commutative, and use associativity to pick the cheaper of (AB)x and A(Bx).

units.title: Linear systems, elimination and inverses
objectives: Write a system of linear equations as Ax = b and solve a 3×3 system by Gaussian elimination.
Decide from the row-echelon form whether a system has no solution, one solution or infinitely many.
Explain when a square matrix is invertible and why numerical code solves Ax = b instead of forming A⁻¹.
State that elimination (LU) on an n×n matrix costs about 2n³/3 operations.

units.title: Span, independence, basis and rank
objectives: Decide whether a set of vectors is linearly independent and find a basis for its span.
Compute the rank of a small matrix by elimination and relate it to the number of independent columns.
State the rank–nullity theorem (rank + nullity = number of columns) and use it to count free variables.
Explain why rank(AB) ≤ min(rank A, rank B), so a product of an m×k and a k×n factor has rank at most k.

units.title: Norms, inner products and orthogonality

State the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality and use it to bound a dot product.
Project a vector onto a line or subspace and explain why the residual is orthogonal to it.
Explain why an orthonormal basis (QᵀQ = I) makes coordinates easy, and measure a weight error with an L2 norm.

State the spectral theorem: a real symmetric matrix has real eigenvalues and orthonormal eigenvectors.
Explain power iteration and why the largest eigenvalue magnitude decides whether repeated products by A grow or shrink.

objectives: State the SVD A = UΣVᵀ, the shapes of U, Σ and V, and that the singular values are square roots of the eigenvalues of AᵀA.

Compute the storage of a rank-k factorization, k(m + n) numbers versus mn, and the largest k that still saves memory.
Compute the energy kept, Σ_{i≤k} σᵢ² / Σ σᵢ², and choose k for a target.
Compress a weight matrix with numpy.linalg.svd and report the relative Frobenius error.

units.title: Tensors, strides and memory layouts
objectives: Describe a tensor by its number of axes, shape and dtype, and compute its size in bytes.
Compute an element's flat memory offset from its indices and strides in row-major (C) order.
Distinguish NCHW from NHWC and explain which loop then reads memory contiguously.
Predict broadcasting results and explain why a transpose returns a view that can be non-contiguous.
Write a batched matrix multiply with einsum.

modules.title: Calculus and optimization
modules.summary: Take derivatives of the functions inside a model, follow the gradient downhill, and know when that search is guaranteed to work.
refs: MML, ch. 5 (Vector Calculus) and ch. 7 (Continuous Optimization)

practice.title: micrograd: build a tiny reverse-mode autodiff engine

units.title: Derivatives as rates of change
objectives: Interpret a derivative as the slope at a point and as the limit of a difference quotient.
Differentiate polynomials, exp and log, and products and quotients with the standard rules.
Derive σ'(x) = σ(x)(1 − σ(x)) for the logistic sigmoid.
Approximate a derivative with a central finite difference and explain the step-size trade-off between truncation and rounding error.

units.title: The chain rule
objectives: State the chain rule for f(g(x)) and apply it to log(1 + eˣ) and σ(wx + b).
Draw a function as a graph of elementary operations and get its derivative by multiplying local derivatives along each path.
Explain why derivatives from several paths add when one variable feeds several operations.
Differentiate a two-layer scalar network by hand.

units.title: Partial derivatives and gradients
objectives: Compute partial derivatives and assemble the gradient vector of a multivariable function.
Explain why the gradient points in the direction of steepest increase and is perpendicular to level sets.
Use the identities ∇ₓ(aᵀx) = a and ∇ₓ(xᵀAx) = (A + Aᵀ)x.
Derive the mean-squared-error gradient for a linear model, (2/n)Xᵀ(Xw − y), and check it numerically.

units.title: Jacobians and automatic differentiation
objectives: Write the Jacobian of a vector-valued function and state its shape (outputs × inputs).
Show that for y = Wx the Jacobian with respect to x is W and that ∂L/∂W = (∂L/∂y)xᵀ.
Explain reverse-mode autodiff as a chain of vector–Jacobian products whose cost is a small constant multiple of one forward pass for a scalar loss.
Say why reverse mode beats forward mode when there are many inputs and one output.
keyTerms: gradient with respect to a matrix

units.title: Taylor series, the Hessian and curvature
objectives: Write first- and second-order Taylor approximations of a function around a point.
Compute the Hessian of a two-variable function and classify a stationary point as minimum, maximum or saddle from its eigenvalues.
Explain how a large ratio of largest to smallest Hessian eigenvalue (condition number) slows gradient descent.
Derive the Newton step −H⁻¹∇f and explain why it is rarely used for large networks.

units.title: Convexity
objectives: Define convex sets and convex functions and test convexity with the second-derivative (Hessian) condition.
State that every local minimum of a convex function is global, and state Jensen's inequality.
Identify which losses are convex in their parameters (least squares, logistic regression) and explain why a neural network's loss is not.

units.title: Gradient descent
objectives: Apply w ← w − η∇L(w) by hand for several steps on a one-dimensional quadratic.
Show that on f(x) = (L/2)x² gradient descent converges only if 0 < η < 2/L, and describe oscillation and divergence.
Explain stochastic and minibatch gradient descent as cheaper, noisy estimates of the full gradient.
Describe momentum as a running average of gradients that speeds progress along consistent directions.
Set up a constrained problem with a Lagrange multiplier and interpret the result.
Implement batch gradient descent for linear regression in NumPy and plot the loss curve.

modules.title: Probability and statistics
modules.summary: Reason about uncertainty: compute probabilities, use Bayes' rule, fit parameters to data, and put error bars on a measured accuracy.
refs: Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability (2nd ed., 2019), ch. 1–10

units.title: Events, conditioning and independence
objectives: Define sample space, event and probability, and use the axioms to compute P(A ∪ B) and P(Aᶜ).
Compute conditional probabilities and test two events for independence.
Count outcomes with the product rule and combinations for simple sampling problems.

units.title: Bayes' rule and base rates
objectives: State Bayes' rule and the law of total probability and name the prior, likelihood and posterior.
Compute the probability that a wake word was really spoken given a detector's hit rate, false-alarm rate and base rate.
Explain the base-rate fallacy: why a detector that is right 99% of the time can still be wrong on most alarms for rare events.

units.title: Random variables and common distributions
objectives: Distinguish discrete and continuous random variables and their PMF, PDF and CDF.
State the parameters and PMF or PDF of the Bernoulli, binomial, categorical, Poisson, uniform and Gaussian distributions.
Pick a distribution for a sensor or count process, such as Poisson for events per second.
Sample from these distributions with numpy.random and compare the histogram with the true PDF.

units.title: Expectation, variance and covariance
objectives: Compute the expectation, variance and standard deviation of discrete and continuous variables.
Use linearity of expectation and Var(aX + b) = a²Var(X), and add variances of independent variables.
Define covariance and correlation and estimate them from samples.
Derive that rounding error uniform over a step Δ has mean 0 and variance Δ²/12.

units.title: Gaussians and the central limit theorem
objectives: Use z-scores and the 68–95–99.7 rule to compute tail probabilities of a normal distribution.
Describe a multivariate Gaussian by its mean vector and covariance matrix, and say what a diagonal covariance means.
State the central limit theorem and explain why averages of many independent errors look Gaussian.
Explain why zero correlation does not imply independence.

units.title: Maximum likelihood and MAP estimation
objectives: Write the log-likelihood of i.i.d. data and find the maximum-likelihood estimate for a Bernoulli and a Gaussian.
Show that minimizing mean squared error is MLE under Gaussian noise and minimizing cross-entropy is MLE for a categorical model.
Derive MAP estimation and show that a Gaussian prior on the weights adds an L2 (weight-decay) penalty.
Update a Beta prior with binomial counts (Beta–binomial conjugacy).

units.title: Standard errors and confidence intervals
objectives: Compute the standard error of a sample mean, σ/√n, and of a measured accuracy, √(p(1 − p)/n).
Build a 95% confidence interval for a test-set accuracy (90% on 1,000 clips gives about ±1.9 points).
Interpret a confidence interval correctly and say what it does not mean.
Estimate an interval by bootstrap resampling in NumPy.

units.title: Comparing two models fairly
objectives: Explain why two models must be compared on the same test set and across several random seeds.
Report mean ± standard deviation over seeds and judge whether a difference is larger than the noise.
Explain the multiple-comparisons problem when you keep the best of many runs or hyperparameter settings.

modules.title: Information theory
modules.summary: Measure information in bits, see why cross-entropy is the standard loss, and estimate how few bits a model's weights really need.
refs: MacKay, Information Theory, Inference, and Learning Algorithms (2003), ch. 1–2, 4–6

units.title: Information content and entropy
objectives: Compute the information content −log₂ p of an outcome and the entropy H(X) = −Σ p log₂ p of a distribution.
Show that entropy is largest (log₂ K bits) for a uniform distribution over K outcomes and zero for a certain outcome.
Convert between bits and nats and compute the entropy of a biased coin.

units.title: Cross-entropy and KL divergence
objectives: Compute the cross-entropy H(p, q) and the KL divergence D_KL(p‖q) for small distributions.
Use H(p, q) = H(p) + D_KL(p‖q) to explain why minimizing cross-entropy against fixed labels minimizes KL.
State Gibbs' inequality (D_KL ≥ 0, zero only when p = q) and show that KL is not symmetric.
Compute the cross-entropy loss of a softmax output for a one-hot label.

units.title: Source coding and Huffman codes
objectives: State the source coding theorem: the average code length cannot beat the entropy, and symbol codes can get within 1 bit of it.
Check codeword lengths with the Kraft inequality and explain why prefix codes decode without separators.
Build a Huffman code by hand for 4–6 symbols and compute its expected length.
Explain how Deep Compression Huffman-codes quantized weight indices to save further storage.

units.title: Bits per weight and model size
objectives: Compute model storage as parameters × bits ÷ 8 (1M weights: 4 MB at 32-bit, 1 MB at 8-bit, 0.5 MB at 4-bit).
Compute the effective bits per weight of a codebook scheme: index bits plus codebook storage spread over all weights.
Explain why the entropy of the quantized-weight histogram bounds what lossless coding can save.
keyTerms: number formats: int8 and int4 storage

modules.title: Signals and DSP
modules.summary: Turn sensor readings into clean digital signals: sample without aliasing, convolve, filter, and see a signal's frequencies with the FFT.
refs: Smith, The Scientist and Engineer's Guide to Digital Signal Processing, ch. 3, 5–12, 14–21
Oppenheim & Willsky, Signals and Systems (2nd ed., 1997), ch. 1–7, 10

units.title: Sampling and quantization
objectives: Relate sampling rate, sample period and samples per window (1 s at 16 kHz is 16,000 samples).
Compute the signal-to-quantization-noise ratio of an ideal N-bit ADC with SNR ≈ 6.02N + 1.76 dB.
Express power and amplitude ratios in decibels.

units.title: Nyquist and aliasing
objectives: State the sampling theorem: a signal band-limited below fs/2 can be rebuilt from its samples.
Compute the aliased frequency of a tone above the Nyquist frequency.
Explain why an analog anti-aliasing filter goes before the ADC and why downsampling needs a digital low-pass first.
Show aliasing in code by sampling a sine wave too slowly.

units.title: LTI systems and convolution
objectives: Define linearity and time invariance and explain why an LTI system is fully described by its impulse response.
Compute a discrete convolution by hand, with output length N + M − 1 and about N·M MACs.
Explain that deep-learning 'convolution' layers compute cross-correlation (no kernel flip).
Implement 1-D convolution with loops and compare it with numpy.convolve.

units.title: Fourier analysis and the DFT
objectives: Write the DFT X[k] = Σ x[n]·e^(−j2πkn/N) and explain it as correlation with complex sinusoids.
Compute the frequency of bin k as k·fs/N and the bin spacing fs/N.
Explain why a real signal's spectrum is conjugate-symmetric, so only N/2 + 1 bins are unique.
State Parseval's relation and compute a magnitude spectrum with numpy.fft.rfft.

units.title: The fast Fourier transform
objectives: Explain how radix-2 Cooley–Tukey splits a DFT into even- and odd-indexed halves recursively.
Compare DFT cost (∝ N²) with FFT cost (∝ N log₂ N) and compute the ratio for N = 512 (about 57×).
Explain that zero-padding interpolates the spectrum but does not add frequency resolution.

units.title: The convolution theorem and FFT convolution
objectives: State the convolution theorem: convolution in time equals multiplication of spectra.
Explain why multiplying DFTs gives circular convolution and how zero-padding to N + M − 1 gives linear convolution.
Estimate the kernel length at which FFT convolution beats direct convolution.

units.title: FIR and IIR filters
objectives: Contrast FIR (feed-forward) and IIR (feedback) filters by cost, phase response and stability.
Write a moving average and a one-pole low-pass y[n] = αx[n] + (1 − α)y[n − 1] as difference equations.
Read cutoff, passband and stopband from a frequency-response plot.
Explain why IIR poles must lie inside the unit circle and why fixed-point MCU code uses cascaded biquads.

units.title: Windowing and spectral leakage
objectives: Explain spectral leakage when a frame does not hold a whole number of periods.
Compare rectangular, Hann and Hamming windows by main-lobe width and side-lobe level.
Compute the frequency resolution fs/N of a frame and choose a frame length for a target resolution.

modules.title: Sensor feature extraction
modules.summary: Turn raw audio, images and motion data into the small feature arrays that tiny models expect, one window at a time.
refs: Edge Impulse docs: processing blocks (spectrogram, MFE, MFCC, image, spectral analysis)

practice.title: Edge Impulse: end-to-end motion recognition with spectral features

units.title: The STFT and spectrograms
objectives: Describe the short-time Fourier transform as framing, windowing and one FFT per frame.
Compute the frame count 1 + ⌊(L − W)/S⌋ (1 s of audio, 30 ms windows, 20 ms stride: 49 frames).
Compute a spectrogram's shape and memory for a given FFT size and frame count.
Explain why log magnitude is used and how frame length trades time resolution for frequency resolution.

units.title: Mel filterbanks, MFE and MFCC
objectives: Convert hertz to mel with m = 2595·log₁₀(1 + f/700) and explain why mel spacing follows human hearing.
Describe the MFE pipeline: power spectrum → triangular mel filterbank → log energies.
Describe MFCC as a DCT of the log mel energies that usually keeps about 13 coefficients.
State the inputs used on MCUs: 49×40 filterbank features in micro_speech and 49×10 MFCCs in the MLPerf Tiny keyword-spotting model.
Explain when Edge Impulse suggests MFCC (human speech) versus MFE (other sounds, convolutional models).
refs: Edge Impulse docs: MFE and MFCC blocks
Banbury et al., MLPerf Tiny Benchmark (arXiv 2106.07597), §4.3

units.title: Image preprocessing for small models
objectives: Resize, center-crop and convert images between RGB and grayscale for a fixed model input.
Normalize pixels for a float model (mean/std or [0, 1]) versus an int8 model (using the input scale and zero-point).
Compute input-buffer memory: 96×96×3 uint8 is 27,648 bytes and 96×96×1 is 9,216 bytes.
Explain how a mismatch in channel order, layout or normalization between training and device silently ruins accuracy.
refs: Banbury et al., MLPerf Tiny Benchmark, §4.1

units.title: Motion (IMU) features
objectives: Describe accelerometer and gyroscope axes, units and typical sampling rates for gesture data.
Compute per-axis window statistics: mean, RMS, standard deviation and peak-to-peak.
Compute per-axis spectral features (band or FFT-bin power) and explain what Edge Impulse's spectral-analysis block outputs.
Remove gravity and drift with a high-pass filter before feature extraction.
refs: Edge Impulse docs: spectral analysis block

units.title: Streaming windows and ring buffers
objectives: Implement a ring buffer that keeps the last W samples and emits a window every S samples.
Compute inference rate and decision latency from window and stride (a 1 s window with 20 ms stride runs 50 times per second).
Reuse features across overlapping windows by computing only the newest frames.
Smooth per-window scores with averaging and a suppression time to cut false triggers.

modules.title: Numerical computing
modules.summary: Keep results accurate in finite precision and see how convolutions are turned into fast matrix multiplies.
refs: Goldberg, What Every Computer Scientist Should Know About Floating-Point Arithmetic (ACM Computing Surveys, 1991)
Goodfellow, Bengio & Courville, Deep Learning (2016), ch. 4
Sze, Chen, Yang & Emer, Efficient Processing of Deep Neural Networks: A Tutorial and Survey (Proc. IEEE, 2017)
Lavin & Gray, Fast Algorithms for Convolutional Neural Networks (CVPR 2016)

units.title: Rounding error and conditioning
objectives: State machine epsilon for fp32 (2⁻²³ ≈ 1.19×10⁻⁷) and fp16 (2⁻¹⁰ ≈ 9.8×10⁻⁴) and the relative rounding-error bound.
Explain catastrophic cancellation and why adding many small values to a large running sum loses them.
Define the condition number κ(A) = σ_max/σ_min and estimate the digits lost as about log₁₀ κ.
keyTerms: number formats: fp32 vs fp16 precision

units.title: Stable softmax and log-sum-exp
objectives: Explain why exp overflows for large logits (above about 88.7 in fp32 and about 11.1 in fp16).
Implement softmax by subtracting the largest logit, and log-sum-exp as m + log Σ exp(xᵢ − m).
Explain why frameworks fuse log-softmax with the negative log-likelihood instead of computing log(softmax(x)).

units.title: im2col: convolution as matrix multiply
objectives: Lower a 2-D convolution to a matrix multiply by unrolling each K×K×C_in input patch into a column (im2col).
Compute the im2col matrix shape, (K·K·C_in) × (H_out·W_out), and its memory blow-up of up to K² times the input.
Explain why tuned GEMM libraries are fast (blocking for caches and registers, data reuse) and why that pays for the extra memory.
refs: Chetlur et al., cuDNN: Efficient Primitives for Deep Learning (arXiv 1410.0759, 2014)

units.title: Winograd and FFT convolution
objectives: Explain how Winograd F(2×2, 3×3) computes a 2×2 output tile with 16 multiplies instead of 36 (2.25× fewer).
Explain why Winograd's input and output transforms add work and can hurt accuracy in low precision such as int8.
Choose between FFT convolution (large kernels), Winograd (small 3×3 kernels) and direct or im2col convolution.

tiers.name: ML and deep learning
tiers.summary: You can build, train and debug classic models and modern neural networks (CNNs, sequence models and transformers) in PyTorch, and explain how today's LLMs and diffusion models are trained and run.

modules.title: ML fundamentals
modules.summary: Frame a learning problem, split the data honestly, fit simple linear models, and judge a classifier with the right metric.
refs: Géron, Hands-On Machine Learning with Scikit-Learn, Keras & TensorFlow (3rd ed., 2022), ch. 1–4
Prince, Understanding Deep Learning (UDL, MIT Press 2023), ch. 1–2, 8–9

units.title: Learning from data and honest splits
objectives: Distinguish supervised, unsupervised and self-supervised learning and name features, labels, parameters and hyperparameters.
Split data into training, validation and test sets and state what each one is for.
Detect data leakage, such as the same speaker or recording session appearing in both training and test data.
Use k-fold cross-validation when data are scarce.

units.title: Linear regression
objectives: Write linear regression ŷ = Xw + b and its mean-squared-error loss.
Solve it with the normal equations w = (XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀy and with gradient descent, and say when each is preferable.
Add polynomial features and explain how a linear model then fits curves.
Implement and train linear regression in NumPy and with scikit-learn.

units.title: Logistic and softmax regression
objectives: Write logistic regression as σ(wᵀx + b) with the binary cross-entropy (log) loss.
Explain why a linear classifier's decision boundary is a hyperplane.
Extend to K classes with a softmax over logits and categorical cross-entropy.
Use the log-loss gradient (ŷ − y)x and train a classifier with scikit-learn.

units.title: Generalization and the bias–variance trade-off
objectives: Recognize underfitting and overfitting from training and validation curves.
State the bias–variance decomposition of expected squared error: bias² + variance + noise.
Explain double descent: test error can fall again once a model is big enough to fit the training data exactly.
Explain why model size is chosen on validation performance, not training loss.

units.title: Regularization
objectives: Add L2 (weight decay) and L1 penalties to a loss and explain why L1 drives some weights exactly to zero.
Use early stopping on validation loss as a regularizer.
Connect an L2 penalty to a Gaussian prior on the weights (MAP).
Tune the regularization strength on a validation set and describe the under- versus over-regularization trade-off.

units.title: Precision, recall and F1
objectives: Build a confusion matrix and compute accuracy, precision, recall and F1 from it.
Explain why accuracy misleads on imbalanced data: a detector that never fires can be 99% accurate.
Move the decision threshold and describe the precision–recall trade-off.
Express wake-word errors as a false-reject rate and false accepts per hour of audio.
Compute per-class and macro-averaged metrics with scikit-learn.

units.title: ROC curves, AUC and calibration
objectives: Draw an ROC curve (true-positive rate against false-positive rate over all thresholds) and read AUC as the chance that a random positive scores above a random negative.
Prefer precision–recall curves over ROC curves when positives are rare.
Explain calibration and read a reliability diagram.
State that MLPerf Tiny scores its anomaly-detection task by ROC AUC with a target of 0.85.
refs: Banbury et al., MLPerf Tiny Benchmark (arXiv 2106.07597), §4.4

modules.title: Classical ML on devices
modules.summary: Use small classic models (nearest neighbors, trees, SVMs, k-means and PCA) that often fit a microcontroller's budget better than a neural network.
refs: Edge Impulse docs: K-means and GMM anomaly-detection blocks

units.title: k-nearest neighbors and distances
objectives: Classify with k-nearest neighbors and explain the roles of k and the distance metric.
Explain why features must be scaled before any distance-based method.
Compute k-NN's memory and per-query cost (store all N training vectors and compute N distances) and why that hurts on an MCU.
Explain the curse of dimensionality for distance-based methods.

units.title: Decision trees, forests and boosting
objectives: Grow a decision tree by picking splits that reduce Gini impurity or entropy, and limit depth to avoid overfitting.
Contrast bagging and random forests with boosting, where each new tree fits the remaining errors of the ensemble.
Estimate a tree's MCU inference cost (one comparison per level) and its size from the node count.
Compare boosted trees with a small neural network on accuracy, memory and latency for tabular sensor features.

units.title: Support vector machines
objectives: Explain the maximum-margin classifier and identify the support vectors.
Write the hinge loss and explain the soft-margin parameter C.
Explain the kernel trick (e.g., the RBF kernel) and why kernel-SVM inference cost grows with the number of support vectors.

units.title: k-means clustering and PCA
objectives: Run k-means (assign points to the nearest centroid, recompute centroids) and choose k with inertia or the silhouette score.
Compute PCA from the SVD or covariance eigenvectors and keep components by explained variance.
Project sensor features onto the top components to shrink a model's input on device.
Use k-means centroids as a codebook, the idea reused later for weight sharing.

units.title: Classical anomaly detection
objectives: Frame anomaly detection as learning what 'normal' looks like from mostly normal data.
Score anomalies by distance to the nearest k-means centroid or by low likelihood under a Gaussian mixture model.
Set a threshold from a percentile of normal validation scores and evaluate with ROC AUC.
Describe Edge Impulse's K-means and GMM anomaly blocks for sensor data.
refs: Edge Impulse docs: K-means and GMM anomaly-detection blocks

modules.title: Neural-network basics
modules.summary: Build a neural network from layers and activations, pick a loss, and compute every gradient with backpropagation.
refs: Stanford CS231n course notes: Backpropagation; Neural Networks Parts 1–3

practice.title: micrograd: an autograd engine and small MLP built from scratch
Stanford CS231n notes: minimal neural network case study

units.title: From perceptrons to MLPs
objectives: Describe a neuron as a dot product plus bias followed by a nonlinearity, and a layer as a matrix multiply.
Explain why stacked linear layers without nonlinearities collapse into one linear map.
State the universal approximation theorem and what it does not promise (size, trainability).
Count a dense layer's parameters, n_in·n_out + n_out, and its MACs per input, n_in·n_out.

units.title: Activation functions
objectives: Define ReLU, leaky ReLU, sigmoid, tanh, GELU and SiLU (Swish) and sketch each.
Explain saturation, why sigmoid and tanh slow learning in deep stacks, and what a dead ReLU is.
Explain why bounded ReLU6 suits int8 deployment and why GELU and SiLU cost more on MCUs (lookup tables or approximations).

units.title: Loss functions
objectives: Derive losses as negative log-likelihoods: MSE for Gaussian outputs, binary cross-entropy for Bernoulli and categorical cross-entropy for softmax outputs.
Compute each loss for a small batch by hand.
Explain label smoothing and class weighting for imbalanced data.
Choose a loss for regression, multi-class and multi-label outputs.

units.title: Computation graphs and backpropagation
objectives: Write an MLP's forward pass as a computation graph and run backpropagation through it with the chain rule.
Derive the dense-layer gradients ∂L/∂W = δxᵀ, ∂L/∂b = δ and ∂L/∂x = Wᵀδ.
Explain why the backward pass costs about twice the forward pass in FLOPs and needs the forward activations kept in memory.
Implement forward and backward for a two-layer MLP in NumPy and check gradients numerically.

units.title: Gradient flow and initialization
objectives: Explain vanishing and exploding gradients as products of many per-layer factors.
State Xavier/Glorot initialization, Var(w) = 2/(n_in + n_out), and He initialization, Var(w) = 2/n_in, and when to use each.
Explain why all-zero initialization fails (symmetry) and why too large a scale blows up activations.
Measure per-layer activation and gradient statistics in code.
refs: Glorot & Bengio, Understanding the Difficulty of Training Deep Feedforward Neural Networks (AISTATS 2010)
He et al., Delving Deep into Rectifiers (ICCV 2015)

units.title: An MLP from scratch in NumPy
objectives: Implement a minibatch training loop for an MLP classifier in NumPy: forward, loss, backward, update.
Overfit a tiny batch first to prove that the code can learn.
Track training and validation loss and accuracy every epoch.
refs: Stanford CS231n notes: Putting it together (minimal neural network case study)

units.title: Parameters, FLOPs and depth
objectives: Separate a network's parameter count, MACs/FLOPs and activation memory, and compute each for a small MLP.
Compute weight storage at fp32 and int8 (4 bytes versus 1 byte per weight).
Explain why deeper networks can represent some functions with far fewer units than shallow ones.
Weigh width against depth for a microcontroller budget of latency, memory and accuracy.
keyTerms: number formats: fp32 vs int8 weights
refs: Telgarsky, Benefits of Depth in Neural Networks (COLT 2016)

modules.title: Training deep networks
modules.summary: Train deep networks reliably: choose an optimizer and learning-rate schedule, normalize and regularize, use mixed precision, and debug runs that fail.
refs: Micikevicius et al., Mixed Precision Training (ICLR 2018)

units.title: Minibatch SGD and momentum
objectives: Define epoch, iteration and batch size, and compute iterations per epoch.
Write SGD with momentum (v ← βv + g; w ← w − ηv) and explain it as a running average of gradients.
Explain how batch size trades gradient noise, throughput and memory, and why larger batches often need a larger learning rate.
Implement momentum SGD in NumPy.

units.title: Adaptive optimizers: RMSProp, Adam and AdamW
objectives: Describe AdaGrad, RMSProp and Adam as per-parameter step sizes built from running averages of squared gradients.
Write the Adam update with first and second moments and bias correction (defaults β₁ = 0.9, β₂ = 0.999).
Explain AdamW's decoupled weight decay and why it differs from adding an L2 term to the loss under Adam.
Compute optimizer memory: Adam stores two extra values (m and v) per parameter.
refs: Loshchilov & Hutter, Decoupled Weight Decay Regularization (ICLR 2019)

units.title: Learning-rate schedules and warmup
objectives: Describe step decay, cosine decay and linear warmup, and sketch the learning rate over a run.
Explain why warmup helps the early training of large models and transformers.
Use a learning-rate range test to choose a starting rate.

units.title: Normalization layers
objectives: Write batch normalization (normalize with batch mean and variance, then scale γ and shift β) and contrast its training and inference behavior.
Explain why LayerNorm and RMSNorm suit transformers and small or variable batches.
Show that at inference batch norm is a per-channel affine map that can be folded into the previous convolution's weights and bias.
Diagnose the bug of evaluating in training mode (batch statistics instead of running averages).

units.title: Dropout and data augmentation
objectives: Explain dropout in training (random zeroing with rescaling) and why it is switched off at inference.
Apply image augmentation (flips, crops, color jitter) and audio augmentation (background-noise mixing, time shift, SpecAugment masking).
Explain mixup and label smoothing as regularizers.
Choose augmentations that keep labels valid for the task.

units.title: Mixed-precision training
objectives: Compare fp32, fp16 and bf16 by exponent and mantissa bits, range and precision.
Explain the fp16 recipe: fp32 master weights, fp16 compute and loss scaling so small gradients do not underflow.
Explain why bf16, with fp32's 8 exponent bits, usually needs no loss scaling.
Estimate the memory and bandwidth saved by 16-bit activations.
keyTerms: number formats: exponent vs mantissa bits
refs: Micikevicius et al., Mixed Precision Training (ICLR 2018)

units.title: Debugging training runs
objectives: Follow a checklist: inspect the data pipeline, overfit one batch, then scale up.
Diagnose failures from loss curves: flat loss (rate too low or a bug), NaNs (rate too high or overflow) and a growing train–validation gap (overfitting).
Monitor gradient norms and apply gradient clipping.
Change one thing at a time and keep a log of runs.
refs: Karpathy, A Recipe for Training Neural Networks (blog, 2019)

modules.title: PyTorch in practice
modules.summary: Write real PyTorch (tensors, autograd, modules and a training loop) and export the trained model for deployment.
refs: PyTorch docs: Autograd mechanics; torch.export; torch.onnx; Automatic Mixed Precision

practice.title: PyTorch tutorial: Learn the Basics (tensors to a full training loop)

units.title: Tensors, dtypes and devices
objectives: Create torch tensors with a given dtype and device and move them between CPU and accelerator.
Reshape with view or reshape, permute axes, and say when .contiguous() is needed.
Convert to and from NumPy and state when memory is shared.
Explain why mixing devices or dtypes in one operation raises errors.

units.title: Autograd in PyTorch
objectives: Use requires_grad and .backward() to compute gradients and read them from .grad.
Explain that gradients accumulate across backward calls and must be zeroed every step.
Use torch.no_grad() or torch.inference_mode() for evaluation, and .detach() to cut a tensor out of the graph.
Explain leaf tensors and why in-place edits of saved tensors can break the backward pass.
refs: PyTorch tutorial: A Gentle Introduction to torch.autograd

units.title: nn.Module, parameters and state_dict

units.title: ResNets and skip connections

units.title: Depthwise-separable and grouped convolutions
objectives: Define depthwise convolution (one K×K filter per channel) and pointwise (1×1) convolution.
Derive the cost ratio of depthwise-separable to standard convolution, 1/N + 1/K², about 8–9× fewer operations for 3×3 kernels.
Explain grouped convolution as the middle ground between standard and depthwise.
Explain why MobileNetV1 spends about 95% of its compute in 1×1 convolutions and what that means for kernel tuning.

units.title: Transfer learning and fine-tuning

Fine-tune more layers at a lower learning rate when more data are available.

units.title: Object detection and YOLO

Compute the IoU of two boxes by hand.
Contrast two-stage detectors (R-CNN family) with one-stage detectors (SSD, YOLO).
Explain YOLO's idea of predicting boxes and classes over a grid in one pass, and why that suits real-time edge use.
Explain mean average precision (mAP) as the standard detection metric.

units.title: The attention mechanism
objectives: Explain attention as a soft lookup: a query is compared with keys and returns a weighted average of values.
Write scaled dot-product attention, softmax(QKᵀ/√d_k)V, with the shapes of Q, K, V and the output.
Explain why scores are divided by √d_k (to keep the softmax out of saturation).
Implement single-head attention in PyTorch and check that each row of weights sums to 1.

units.title: Self-attention and masking
objectives: Distinguish self-attention from cross-attention.

Compute the memory of the n×n score matrix and explain its quadratic growth with sequence length.

units.title: Multi-head and grouped-query attention
objectives: Explain multi-head attention: h heads of size d_model/h, concatenated and mixed by an output projection.

Describe multi-query attention (one shared K/V head) and grouped-query attention (groups of query heads share K/V).
Explain how GQA shrinks the KV cache and memory traffic at a small accuracy cost.
