units.title: The transformer block
objectives: Draw a transformer block: attention and a feed-forward network (usually 4× wider), each wrapped in a residual connection and normalization.
Contrast pre-norm and post-norm placement and explain why pre-norm trains more stably in deep stacks.
Distinguish encoder-only (BERT), decoder-only (GPT) and encoder–decoder transformers.
Name SwiGLU feed-forward layers and RMSNorm as common modern substitutions.

units.title: Positional encodings and RoPE
objectives: Describe sinusoidal and learned absolute position embeddings.
Explain rotary position embedding (RoPE): rotate each pair of query/key dimensions by a position-dependent angle so scores depend on relative offset.
Compute RoPE frequencies θᵢ = 10000^(−2i/d) for a small d.
Explain why the position scheme matters when running past the training context length.
refs: Su et al., RoFormer: Enhanced Transformer with Rotary Position Embedding (arXiv 2104.09864, 2021)

units.title: Vision transformers
objectives: Turn an image into tokens: split into 16×16 patches, flatten and project, add a class token and position embeddings.
Compute the token count for a 224×224 input with 16×16 patches (196 patches plus 1 class token).
Explain why ViTs need more data or distillation than CNNs (weaker built-in locality bias) and why CNN–transformer hybrids are popular on the edge.
refs: Dosovitskiy et al., An Image is Worth 16x16 Words (ICLR 2021)

units.title: Transformer FLOPs and memory
objectives: Count parameters per layer as about 12·d_model² (4d² for attention projections plus 8d² for a 4× feed-forward).
Estimate forward compute as about 2 FLOPs per parameter per token and training as about 6 (Kaplan et al., 2020).
Add the attention-score cost, which grows with context length, and find when it rivals the weight FLOPs.
Contrast prefill (many tokens at once, compute-heavy) with decode (one token at a time, limited by memory traffic).
Compute a small GPT's parameter count and per-token FLOPs in Python.
refs: Kaplan et al., Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models (arXiv 2001.08361, 2020)
Raschka, LLMs-from-scratch repository: FLOPs analysis (bonus material, ch. 4)

units.title: The KV cache
objectives: Explain why autoregressive decoding would recompute past keys and values without a cache.
Compute KV-cache size as 2 × layers × KV heads × head dim × tokens × bytes per value.
Work an example: 32 layers, 8 KV heads of dim 128, 4,096 tokens in fp16 gives 512 MiB per sequence.
Explain how GQA/MQA, cache quantization and sliding windows shrink the cache, and why the cache limits long contexts on edge devices.
Add a KV cache to a small GPT and measure the decode speed-up.
refs: Raschka, LLMs-from-scratch repository: KV cache (bonus material, ch. 4)

units.title: Tokenization and byte-pair encoding
objectives: Explain why text is split into subword tokens rather than characters or whole words.
Run byte-pair encoding by hand: start from bytes or characters and repeatedly merge the most frequent adjacent pair.
Compute the embedding table size, vocabulary × d_model, and its share of a small model's parameters.
Explain the vocabulary-size trade-off: shorter sequences versus bigger embedding and output layers.
refs: Sennrich, Haddow & Birch, Neural Machine Translation of Rare Words with Subword Units (ACL 2016)
Stanford CS224n (Winter 2026), guest lecture 'Tokenization and Multilinguality'

units.title: Language modeling and pretraining
objectives: Define a causal language model as next-token prediction trained with cross-entropy on shifted sequences.
Compute perplexity as exp(average cross-entropy in nats).
Contrast GPT-style next-token pretraining with BERT-style masked-token pretraining.
Pretrain a tiny GPT on a small text corpus and sample from it.

units.title: Decoding strategies and generation latency
objectives: Describe greedy decoding, beam search, temperature sampling, top-k and top-p (nucleus) sampling.
Explain how temperature reshapes the softmax and why a temperature near 0 approaches greedy decoding.
Explain why greedy and beam search tend to repeat themselves in open-ended generation.
Define time to first token (TTFT) and time per output token (TPOT) as generation latency metrics.
Implement top-k and top-p sampling in PyTorch.
refs: Holtzman et al., The Curious Case of Neural Text Degeneration (ICLR 2020)

units.title: Scaling laws
objectives: State that language-model loss falls as a power law in parameters, data and compute (Kaplan et al., 2020).
Use C ≈ 6·N·D to estimate training compute from parameters N and training tokens D.
Apply the Chinchilla result: compute-optimal training uses about 20 tokens per parameter.
Explain why small edge models are trained on far more tokens than compute-optimal (cheaper inference later).
refs: Hoffmann et al., Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models (arXiv 2203.15556, 2022)

units.title: Fine-tuning, SFT and LoRA
objectives: Contrast classification fine-tuning (a new head) with instruction fine-tuning (SFT on prompt–response pairs).
Explain the memory cost of full fine-tuning: weights, gradients and optimizer state.
Explain LoRA: freeze W and learn a low-rank update BA of rank r, adding r·(d + k) parameters per d×k matrix.
Fine-tune a small GPT with LoRA and merge the adapter into the weights for inference.
refs: Hu et al., LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models (ICLR 2022)

units.title: Preference tuning: RLHF and DPO
objectives: Describe the RLHF pipeline: SFT, a reward model trained on human preference pairs, then RL (PPO) with a KL penalty toward the SFT model.
Explain DPO: train the policy directly on preference pairs with a classification-style loss, with no separate reward model or RL loop.
Explain why a KL penalty keeps the tuned model close to the reference model.
Name InstructGPT (2022) and DPO (2023) as the landmark methods.
refs: Ouyang et al., Training Language Models to Follow Instructions with Human Feedback (NeurIPS 2022)
Rafailov et al., Direct Preference Optimization (NeurIPS 2023)
Raschka, LLMs-from-scratch repository: DPO bonus material (ch. 7)

units.title: Diffusion models
objectives: Describe the forward process (gradually add Gaussian noise) and the learned reverse process (remove it step by step).
State the DDPM training objective: predict the added noise with a mean-squared-error loss.
Explain latent diffusion and classifier-free guidance.
Explain why sampling costs (number of steps) × (denoiser cost) and how fewer-step samplers and distillation cut it for devices.
Place diffusion models relative to GANs and VAEs.
refs: UDL, ch. 18 (and ch. 15 and 17 for GANs and VAEs)
Ho, Jain & Abbeel, Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (NeurIPS 2020)

modules.title: Efficiency metrics

Sze, Chen, Yang & Emer, Efficient Processing of Deep Neural Networks: A Tutorial and Survey (Proc. IEEE, 2017)
Horowitz, Computing's Energy Problem (and What We Can Do About It) (ISSCC 2014)

units.title: Why efficiency matters at the edge
objectives: List the reasons to run models on the device: latency, privacy, bandwidth, cost, energy and working offline.
Place device classes on a memory scale: MCUs with hundreds of KB of SRAM versus phones and edge SoCs with GB of DRAM.
Explain why model size and compute grew faster than hardware efficiency, which motivates compression.
Weigh on-device against cloud inference for a given product.
keyTerms: memory hierarchy: KB of SRAM vs GB of DRAM

units.title: Parameters, model size, MACs and FLOPs
objectives: Distinguish parameter count, model size (parameters × bit width), MACs, FLOPs (≈ 2 × MACs) and FLOPS (a rate).
Compute MACs for dense, convolution, depthwise and attention layers from their shapes.
Compute a model's size at fp32, fp16, int8 and int4.
Profile parameters and MACs per layer of a PyTorch model and find the heaviest layers.
refs: MIT 6.5940 (Fall 2024) Lecture 2: Basics of Deep Learning

units.title: Latency, throughput and batching
objectives: Define latency (time per inference) and throughput (inferences per second) and explain why batching raises throughput but also latency.
Apply Little's law (items in flight = throughput × latency) to a simple pipeline.
Explain why fewer MACs do not guarantee lower latency (memory traffic, parallelism, kernel support).
Measure latency properly: warm-up runs, many repetitions, and percentiles (p50, p90, p99).

units.title: Weights, activations and peak memory
objectives: Separate weight memory (read-only, can stay in flash) from activation memory (read-write, must fit in SRAM).
Compute peak activation memory as the largest total of tensors alive at once (for a plain chain, the maximum over layers of input + output).
Show that the early high-resolution layers of MobileNet-style networks set the peak, so memory use is very uneven across layers.
Explain how skip connections and execution order change which tensors are alive.
Compute per-layer activation sizes in code and find the peak.
refs: Lin et al., MCUNetV2: Memory-Efficient Patch-based Inference for Tiny Deep Learning (NeurIPS 2021)

units.title: Energy per operation and data movement
objectives: Recall Horowitz's 45 nm table: 32-bit int add 0.1 pJ, fp32 add 0.9 pJ, 32-bit int multiply 3.1 pJ, fp32 multiply 3.7 pJ; 8-bit int add 0.03 pJ and multiply 0.2 pJ.

Recall memory costs: a 64-bit read costs 10 pJ from an 8 KB cache, 20 pJ from 32 KB, 100 pJ from 1 MB and 1.3–2.6 nJ from DRAM; per 32-bit word that is about 5 pJ from a small SRAM versus 640 pJ from DRAM.
Estimate inference energy as Σ(operations × energy per op) + Σ(accesses × energy per access) and show that data movement dominates.
Explain why lower precision saves energy twice: cheaper arithmetic and fewer bytes moved.
keyTerms: number formats: energy vs bit width
refs: Han et al., Learning both Weights and Connections for Efficient Neural Networks (NIPS 2015)

units.title: Arithmetic intensity
objectives: Define arithmetic intensity as operations per byte moved between memory and compute.
Compute the intensity of a matrix multiply (2MNK operations over the bytes of all three matrices) and of a matrix–vector product (about 2 operations per weight byte at int8, 0.5 at fp32).
Explain how batching and data reuse (weight, input and output reuse) raise intensity, and why depthwise and fully connected layers have low intensity.
Compute per-layer intensity for a CNN in code.

units.title: A first roofline
objectives: Write the roofline: attainable performance = min(peak compute, memory bandwidth × arithmetic intensity).
Compute the ridge point (peak compute ÷ bandwidth) and classify a layer as memory-bound or compute-bound.
Build a roofline for a microcontroller from MACs per cycle, clock rate and SRAM or flash bandwidth, and place DS-CNN layers on it.
Pick optimizations for each side: reuse and fusion when memory-bound, SIMD and lower precision when compute-bound.

units.title: Memory hierarchy, tiling and dataflow
objectives: Order the levels (registers, SRAM or cache, flash or DRAM) by size, bandwidth and energy per access.
Explain tiling: work on blocks small enough to stay in fast memory and reuse them before eviction.
Describe weight-stationary, output-stationary and row-stationary (Eyeriss) dataflows as choices of which data stays in place.
Explain how NHWC versus NCHW layouts change contiguous access for depthwise and pointwise kernels.
refs: Chen, Emer & Sze, Eyeriss: A Spatial Architecture for Energy-Efficient Dataflow for CNNs (ISCA 2016)

Choose per-layer ratios from the scan, pruning robust layers more and sensitive layers less.
Use a gradual schedule that raises sparsity step by step during fine-tuning.
Explain AMC: reinforcement learning picks per-layer ratios with latency or FLOPs in the reward.
refs: MIT 6.5940 Lecture 4: Pruning and Sparsity (Part II)
He et al., AMC: AutoML for Model Compression and Acceleration on Mobile Devices (ECCV 2018)
Zhu & Gupta, To Prune, or Not to Prune (arXiv 1710.01878, 2017)

units.title: The lottery ticket hypothesis
objectives: State the hypothesis: dense, randomly initialized networks contain sparse subnetworks that, trained alone from their original initialization, reach comparable accuracy.
Describe iterative magnitude pruning with weight rewinding to find a winning ticket.
Recall that Frankle and Carbin found winning tickets under 10–20% of the original size for MNIST and CIFAR-10 networks.
Explain why finding tickets needs repeated training, so it does not by itself make training cheaper.
refs: Frankle & Carbin, The Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (ICLR 2019)

units.title: The Deep Compression pipeline
objectives: Describe Deep Compression's three stages: pruning, trained quantization (weight sharing) and Huffman coding.
Recall the results: AlexNet 240 MB → 6.9 MB (35×) and VGG-16 552 MB → 11.3 MB (49×) with no accuracy loss.
Compute one layer's compressed size from its sparsity, index bits, codebook bits and Huffman savings.
Explain why compressed weights need decoding or a dedicated accelerator (EIE) to run fast.
refs: Han et al., EIE: Efficient Inference Engine on Compressed Deep Neural Network (ISCA 2016)

units.title: N:M and 2:4 structured sparsity
objectives: Define N:M sparsity and the 2:4 pattern: in every group of 4 consecutive weights, at least 2 are zero.
State that NVIDIA's Ampere sparse tensor cores use the 2:4 pattern to double math throughput over dense tensor cores.
Compute 2:4 storage: half the values plus a 2-bit position index for each kept value.
Describe the recipe: train dense, prune to 2:4 by magnitude, then retrain with the mask fixed.
Explain why end-to-end speed-ups fall below 2× (memory-bound layers and non-matrix operations).
refs: Mishra et al., Accelerating Sparse Deep Neural Networks (arXiv 2104.08378, 2021)

units.title: Making sparsity pay off on devices
objectives: Explain when sparsity speeds things up: structured pruning always, unstructured only with sparse kernels at high sparsity.
Explain why unstructured sparsity rarely speeds up int8 kernels on a Cortex-M, while channel pruning shrinks both flash and latency.
Prune a model with the PyTorch or TensorFlow Model Optimization pruning APIs and make the pruning permanent.
Measure the real latency and size change on the target instead of trusting the sparsity percentage.

modules.title: Quantization I
modules.summary: Store and compute with 8-bit integers instead of 32-bit floats: the scale and zero-point math, calibration, and integer-only kernels.
refs: Jacob et al., Quantization and Training of Neural Networks for Efficient Integer-Arithmetic-Only Inference (CVPR 2018)
Nagel et al., A White Paper on Neural Network Quantization (arXiv 2106.08295, 2021)
LiteRT docs: quantization specification; post-training quantization

practice.title: MIT 6.5940 (Fall 2024) Lab 2: Quantization (Colab)

units.title: Why quantize
objectives: List quantization's gains: 4× smaller weights (fp32 → int8), less memory traffic and cheaper integer arithmetic.
Compare 45 nm energies: an 8-bit multiply costs 0.2 pJ versus 3.7 pJ for fp32 (about 18×).
Recall the formats involved: two's-complement int8 and uint8, fixed point, and fp32, fp16 and bf16.
Explain why int8 is the native format of MCU kernels (CMSIS-NN) and of most NPUs.

units.title: K-means quantization and weight sharing
objectives: Quantize a weight matrix with k-means: store a codebook of k centroids and a log₂k-bit index per weight.
Compute storage as N·log₂k bits of indices plus 32·k bits of codebook.
Explain fine-tuning the centroids by summing the gradients of all weights that share one.
Explain why weight sharing saves storage but not arithmetic (weights are decoded to floats before use).

units.title: The affine scheme r = S(q − Z)
objectives: Write the affine map r = S(q − Z) and the quantizer q = clamp(round(r/S) + Z, q_min, q_max).
Compute S = (r_max − r_min)/(q_max − q_min) and Z = round(q_min − r_min/S) for a given range.
Explain why real 0 must map exactly to an integer (zero padding, ReLU zeros).
Quantize and dequantize a tensor in NumPy and check that the error inside the range is at most S/2.
Explain the trade-off between a wide range (less clipping) and a small step (finer resolution).

units.title: Symmetric versus asymmetric quantization
objectives: Define symmetric quantization (Z = 0, S = max|r|/127) with the restricted int8 range [−127, 127].
Explain why asymmetric quantization suits one-sided data such as ReLU outputs.
Show the extra cross terms a nonzero weight zero-point adds to the integer matrix multiply, and why weights are usually symmetric.
Explain power-of-two scales as a hardware-friendly special case.

units.title: Per-tensor versus per-channel scales
objectives: Contrast per-tensor, per-channel (one scale per output channel) and per-group quantization.
Explain why depthwise convolutions with very different channel ranges lose accuracy under a single per-tensor scale.

State the LiteRT int8 convention: weights symmetric (zero-point 0, values in [−127, 127]) with per-axis scales; activations asymmetric per tensor in [−128, 127]; biases int32 with scale = input scale × weight scale.
Compute the extra storage and requantization work that per-channel scales add.
refs: Krishnamoorthi, Quantizing Deep Convolutional Networks for Efficient Inference: A Whitepaper (arXiv 1806.08342, 2018)

units.title: Calibration and range setting
objectives: Run post-training quantization: feed a representative calibration set and record activation ranges.
Compare range setters (min–max, percentile, MSE-minimizing, KL/entropy) and the clipping-versus-rounding error trade-off.
Explain cross-layer equalization, bias correction and AdaRound as PTQ refinements, in the order of Nagel et al.'s standard pipeline.
Explain why a small representative set (typically hundreds of samples) usually suffices and why unrepresentative samples fail.

units.title: Integer-only inference and requantization
objectives: Expand q₃ = Z₃ + (S₁S₂/S₃)·Σ(q₁ − Z₁)(q₂ − Z₂) and show which zero-point terms can be precomputed.
Explain int32 accumulators and int32 biases with scale S₁S₂ and zero-point 0.
Write the multiplier M = S₁S₂/S₃ as 2⁻ⁿ·M₀ with M₀ in [0.5, 1) stored as a 32-bit fixed-point integer, and apply it with a fixed-point multiply and a rounding right shift.
Fuse ReLU or ReLU6 into the final clamp before saturating to int8.
Implement an integer-only matrix multiply with requantization in C or NumPy that matches the float result to within one quantization step.

units.title: Batch-norm folding and operator fusion
objectives: Fold batch norm into a convolution: w' = γw/√(σ² + ε) and b' = β + γ(b − μ)/√(σ² + ε).
Explain why folding happens before quantization, so the folded weights are the ones quantized.
Fuse convolution, bias and ReLU into one kernel and explain the memory traffic saved.
Explain why folding can widen per-channel weight ranges and favors per-channel scales.

units.title: Post-training quantization in practice
objectives: Produce a fully integer .tflite model (int8 inputs and outputs) with the LiteRT converter and a representative dataset.
Quantize a PyTorch model with an export-based post-training flow (torch.export plus a quantizer, e.g. via torchao) or through ONNX Runtime's quantization tools.
Debug accuracy loss by comparing float and quantized outputs layer by layer and keeping sensitive layers at higher precision.
Recall that MLPerf Tiny's closed division allows post-training quantization with the provided calibration data but not retraining.
refs: Banbury et al., MLPerf Tiny Benchmark, §5.2

modules.title: Quantization II
modules.summary: Go below 8 bits and train for it: quantization-aware training, mixed precision, 4-bit and binary weights, FP8, and quantizing LLMs.
refs: MIT 6.5940 Lecture 6: Quantization (Part II), and Fall 2024 Lecture 13: Efficient LLM Deployment
Micikevicius et al., FP8 Formats for Deep Learning (arXiv 2209.05433, 2022)

practice.title: MIT 6.5940 (Fall 2024) Lab 4: LLM compression (Colab)
TensorFlow Model Optimization guide: quantization-aware training

units.title: Quantization-aware training
objectives: Explain QAT: insert fake-quantize (quantize then dequantize) operations so training sees rounding and clipping.
Follow the recipe: start from a trained float model with PTQ-initialized ranges and fine-tune briefly at a low learning rate with batch norm folded.
Decide when QAT is worth it: below 8 bits, compact depthwise models, or when PTQ loses too much accuracy.
Set up QAT with a framework API and compare it against PTQ.
refs: TensorFlow Model Optimization guide: quantization-aware training

units.title: The straight-through estimator
objectives: Explain why rounding has zero gradient almost everywhere, which would stop learning.
Apply the straight-through estimator: treat round() as the identity in the backward pass and pass gradients only inside the clamp range.
Explain learned step sizes (LSQ) and learned clipping (PACT) as trainable quantizer parameters.
refs: Bengio, Léonard & Courville, Estimating or Propagating Gradients Through Stochastic Neurons (arXiv 1308.3432, 2013)
Esser et al., Learned Step Size Quantization (ICLR 2020)

units.title: Mixed-precision quantization
objectives: Explain mixed-precision quantization: different bit widths for different layers.
Count the search space (b choices per layer over L layers gives b^L configurations) and why search or sensitivity heuristics are needed.
Explain Hessian-based sensitivity (HAWQ) and hardware-in-the-loop search (HAQ).
Weigh accuracy against latency and energy, noting that the hardware must support each bit width for any gain.
refs: Wang et al., HAQ: Hardware-Aware Automated Quantization with Mixed Precision (CVPR 2019)
Dong et al., HAWQ: Hessian AWare Quantization (ICCV 2019)

units.title: INT4, binary and ternary weights
objectives: Pack two int4 values per byte and compute the size of a 4-bit model with group-wise scales (one fp16 scale per 128 weights adds 0.125 bits per weight).
Explain weight-only int4 quantization (activations stay 16-bit) and why it speeds up memory-bound decoding.
Describe binary networks (weights ±1, so XNOR and popcount replace multiply-accumulate) and ternary weights (−1, 0, +1).
Explain the accuracy cliff at 1–2 bits and the usual fixes (keep the first and last layers at higher precision, widen layers).

units.title: FP8: E4M3 and E5M2
objectives: Decode E4M3 (exponent bias 7, max 448, no infinities, a single NaN pattern) and E5M2 (bias 15, max 57,344, IEEE-style infinities and NaNs).
Explain the recommended split: E4M3 for weights and activations, E5M2 for gradients.
Explain why FP8 needs per-tensor scaling factors to fit values into its range.
Compare FP8 with INT8 for inference: wider dynamic range versus uniform resolution and simpler integer hardware.
refs: Micikevicius et al., FP8 Formats for Deep Learning (arXiv 2209.05433, 2022), Table 1

units.title: SQNR and quantization error analysis
objectives: Define SQNR = 10·log₁₀(signal power / quantization-noise power) in decibels.
Use the uniform-noise variance Δ²/12 to derive the rule of about 6 dB more SQNR per extra bit.
Compute per-layer SQNR between float and quantized outputs to find where accuracy is lost.
Explain how outliers stretch the range and lower SQNR for every other value.

units.title: Quantizing LLMs
objectives: Explain activation outliers in LLMs and why naive W8A8 quantization fails (LLM.int8() keeps outlier features in 16-bit).
Explain SmoothQuant: rescale channels to move quantization difficulty from activations to weights.
Explain weight-only methods (GPTQ, AWQ) and why W4A16 suits memory-bound on-device decoding.
Estimate the weight memory of a 1B-parameter model at fp16, int8 and int4 (about 2, 1 and 0.5 GB).

modules.title: Efficient architectures and NAS
modules.summary: Design networks that are efficient by construction, and let a search find the best architecture for a given device's latency and memory.
refs: MIT 6.5940 Lectures 7–8: Neural Architecture Search (Parts I–II), and Lecture 10: MCUNet
Howard et al., MobileNets (arXiv 1704.04861, 2017); Sandler et al., MobileNetV2 (CVPR 2018)
Lin et al., MCUNet: Tiny Deep Learning on IoT Devices (NeurIPS 2020)

practice.title: MIT 6.5940 (Fall 2024) Lab 3: Neural architecture search (Colab)
Once-for-All: pretrained supernets and specialization code

units.title: Efficient building blocks
objectives: Compare the MACs and parameters of standard, grouped, depthwise-separable and 1×1 convolutions for the same shapes.
Describe the inverted residual block (1×1 expand, 3×3 depthwise, 1×1 linear projection) and why its bottleneck is linear.
Explain squeeze-and-excitation and channel shuffle as cheap accuracy boosters.
Explain why inverted residuals create large intermediate activations, which matters for SRAM.
keyTerms: memory hierarchy: activation peaks inside blocks
refs: Sandler et al., MobileNetV2: Inverted Residuals and Linear Bottlenecks (CVPR 2018)

units.title: The MobileNet family
objectives: Trace MobileNetV1 (depthwise-separable convolutions), V2 (inverted residuals, linear bottlenecks) and V3 (search-designed, h-swish, SE blocks).
Apply the width multiplier α (cost falls by about α²) and the resolution multiplier ρ (cost falls by ρ²).
Explain why MobileNetV1 at width 0.25 is the MLPerf Tiny visual-wake-words reference.
Pick a MobileNet variant and multipliers for a given flash and SRAM budget.
refs: Howard et al., Searching for MobileNetV3 (ICCV 2019)

units.title: EfficientNet and compound scaling
objectives: Write compound scaling: depth d = α^φ, width w = β^φ, resolution r = γ^φ with α·β²·γ² ≈ 2, so FLOPs grow by about 2^φ.
Recall the searched values α = 1.2, β = 1.1, γ = 1.15 and the B0 baseline (0.39B FLOPs, 77.1% top-1).
Compute the FLOPs multiplier for a given φ.
Explain why scaling resolution is costly on MCUs: activation memory grows with r².
refs: Tan & Le, EfficientNet: Rethinking Model Scaling for Convolutional Neural Networks (ICML 2019)

units.title: NAS: search spaces and strategies
objectives: Describe NAS as a search space, a search strategy and a performance estimator.
Contrast cell-level and network-level search spaces.
Compare search strategies: reinforcement learning (Zoph & Le), evolution, gradient-based (DARTS) and random search.
Explain why early NAS cost thousands of GPU-days and how weight sharing and proxy tasks cut that cost.
refs: Zoph & Le, Neural Architecture Search with Reinforcement Learning (ICLR 2017)
Liu, Simonyan & Yang, DARTS: Differentiable Architecture Search (ICLR 2019)

units.title: One-shot NAS and weight sharing
objectives: Explain a supernet: one over-parameterized network whose subnetworks share weights, so candidates can be scored without training each one.
Describe ProxylessNAS: search directly on the target task and hardware, using path binarization to keep memory low.
Explain why weight-sharing rankings can disagree with stand-alone training.
Count the candidates in a layer-wise search space (6 choices in each of 20 layers gives 6²⁰ ≈ 3.7×10¹⁵).
refs: Cai, Zhu & Han, ProxylessNAS: Direct Neural Architecture Search on Target Task and Hardware (ICLR 2019)

units.title: Once-for-All networks
objectives: Explain Once-for-All: train one network once, then pick a specialized subnetwork for each device without retraining.
Describe progressive shrinking over kernel size, depth, width and resolution.
Recall the claims: more than 10¹⁹ subnetworks and 80.0% ImageNet top-1 under 600M MACs.
Search a pretrained OFA network for a latency target with an accuracy predictor and a latency lookup table.
keyTerms: elastic kernel, depth, width and resolution
refs: Cai et al., Once-for-All: Train One Network and Specialize It for Efficient Deployment (ICLR 2020)

units.title: Hardware-aware search
objectives: Explain why the search must use measured latency or energy on the target device rather than MACs.
Build a per-operator latency lookup table and sum it to predict a network's latency.
Use a multi-objective reward such as MnasNet's ACC × (LAT/T)^w and read a Pareto front.
Explain why the best network differs across CPU, GPU, MCU and NPU targets.
refs: Tan et al., MnasNet: Platform-Aware Neural Architecture Search for Mobile (CVPR 2019)

units.title: TinyNAS and MCUNet
objectives: Explain TinyNAS's two stages: first optimize the search space (input resolution and width) to fit the MCU's memory, then search a network inside it.
Explain system–model co-design: TinyNAS and the TinyEngine inference library are designed together.
Recall MCUNet's result: over 70% ImageNet top-1 on an off-the-shelf MCU, with 3.5× less SRAM and 5.7× less flash than quantized MobileNetV2 and ResNet-18.
Size a search space for an STM32F746-class MCU (320 KB SRAM, 1 MB flash).
refs: Lin et al., MCUNet: Tiny Deep Learning on IoT Devices (NeurIPS 2020)

modules.title: Distillation and low-rank
modules.summary: Train a small student network to imitate a large teacher, and split big weight matrices into smaller low-rank pieces.
refs: Hinton, Vinyals & Dean, Distilling the Knowledge in a Neural Network (arXiv 1503.02531, 2015)
Hu et al., LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models (ICLR 2022)

units.title: Knowledge distillation
objectives: Explain teacher–student distillation and why soft targets carry 'dark knowledge' about which classes resemble each other.
Write softmax with temperature, qᵢ = exp(zᵢ/T)/Σⱼ exp(zⱼ/T), and compute it at T = 1 and T = 4.
Write the loss α·T²·KL(teacher_T ‖ student_T) + (1 − α)·CE(labels, student) and explain the T² factor (soft-target gradients shrink as 1/T²).
Recall Hinton et al.'s MNIST result: a small net made 146 test errors alone and 74 when trained on soft targets at T = 20.
Implement a distillation loss in PyTorch.

units.title: Feature, attention and relational distillation
objectives: List what a student can match besides logits: intermediate features (FitNets hints), attention maps and relations between samples.
Explain self-distillation and online (mutual) distillation, which need no separately pretrained teacher.
Explain why tiny models benefit most and how network augmentation (training a tiny model inside a larger one) differs from distillation.
Apply distillation to a keyword-spotting or detection student.
refs: Romero et al., FitNets: Hints for Thin Deep Nets (ICLR 2015)
Zagoruyko & Komodakis, Paying More Attention to Attention (ICLR 2017)

units.title: Low-rank factorization of layers
objectives: Replace an m×n weight matrix by m×k and k×n factors from a truncated SVD, cutting parameters from mn to k(m + n).
Find the break-even rank k < mn/(m + n) and choose k from the singular-value energy.
Factor convolutions spatially (k×1 then 1×k) or across channels, then fine-tune to recover accuracy.
Explain why fewer MACs from factoring may not cut latency (two small kernels, extra memory traffic).
Factor a model's dense layers in PyTorch and measure accuracy, size and latency.
refs: Denton et al., Exploiting Linear Structure Within Convolutional Networks for Efficient Evaluation (NIPS 2014)
Jaderberg, Vedaldi & Zisserman, Speeding up Convolutional Neural Networks with Low Rank Expansions (BMVC 2014)

units.title: LoRA and combining compression techniques
objectives: Explain LoRA as a low-rank update W + BA (rank r much smaller than d) and compute its trainable parameters, r(d + k).
Explain why a merged LoRA adapter adds no inference latency.
Order compression steps (distill or prune, then quantize, then compile) and explain why the order matters.
Read an accuracy–efficiency frontier to choose a combined recipe.
refs: Raschka, Build a Large Language Model (From Scratch), App. E

modules.title: MCU inference engines
modules.summary: Run quantized models on microcontrollers: how LiteRT for Microcontrollers manages memory, how optimized kernels and code generators speed it up, and how to fit models into tiny SRAM.
refs: MIT 6.5940 Lectures 10–11: MCUNet; TinyEngine and Parallel Processing
David et al., TensorFlow Lite Micro: Embedded Machine Learning on TinyML Systems (MLSys 2021)
LiteRT for Microcontrollers docs: overview; get started
Lin et al., MCUNetV2: Memory-Efficient Patch-based Inference for Tiny Deep Learning (NeurIPS 2021)

practice.title: Capstone: keyword spotting on a Cortex-M board, starting from the TFLM micro_speech example
Capstone hardware path: micro_speech on the Arduino Nano 33 BLE Sense (Cortex-M4F)
Capstone alternative: Edge Impulse keyword-spotting tutorial (deploy to a Cortex-M board)
TinyEngine: MIT's memory-efficient MCU inference library

units.title: MCU memory budgets
objectives: Map a model onto MCU memory: weights and code in flash (read-only), the tensor arena with activations in SRAM.
Recall typical budgets: STM32F746 with 320 KB SRAM and 1 MB flash; nRF52840 with 256 KB SRAM and 1 MB flash.
Check whether a model fits: weights within the flash left after code, and peak activations plus runtime overhead within the SRAM left by the application.
Weigh reading weights directly from flash (slower, with wait states) against copying hot data into SRAM.

units.title: Inside LiteRT for Microcontrollers
objectives: Explain LiteRT for Microcontrollers (formerly TensorFlow Lite Micro): an interpreter reads a FlatBuffer model from flash and runs its topologically sorted operators in a loop.
Explain the OpResolver: the application registers only the kernels it needs, which keeps the binary small.
Recall the design limits: no OS, no dynamic allocation after initialization, no standard library required, a subset of operators and no on-device training.
Recall measured footprints: the core runtime fits in 16 KB on a Cortex-M3; interpreter overhead was under 0.1% for VWW and 3.3–4.1% for a small hotword model on a Cortex-M4.

units.title: The tensor arena and memory planning
objectives: Explain the tensor arena: one fixed buffer supplied by the application, from which all tensors are allocated at initialization.
Explain the two-stack scheme: interpreter-lifetime (persistent) allocations grow from one end and function-lifetime (non-persistent) allocations from the other.
Explain the memory planner's greedy first-fit-decreasing packing of tensors whose lifetimes do not overlap, and offline-planned layouts stored in the model.
Right-size the arena by calling AllocateTensors() and reading arena_used_bytes(), then adding a margin.
Explain how several models can share one arena (multitenancy).
refs: LiteRT for Microcontrollers docs: get started

units.title: Running a model on a Cortex-M
objectives: Embed a .tflite model as a C array, build a MicroInterpreter with a resolver and an arena, and call AllocateTensors() and Invoke().
Quantize inputs with the input tensor's scale and zero-point, and dequantize outputs before use.
Debug common failures: a missing operator registration, an arena that is too small, unaligned model data, and float inputs fed to an int8 model.
Time Invoke() with a cycle counter or the micro profiler.
refs: LiteRT for Microcontrollers docs: get started

units.title: CMSIS-NN, SIMD and Helium
objectives: Explain CMSIS-NN's three tiers: pure C for any Cortex-M, DSP-extension SIMD (e.g., Cortex-M4, M7, M33) and MVE/Helium vectors (Cortex-M55, M85).
Explain how a dual 16-bit multiply-accumulate (SMLAD) doubles int8 MAC throughput once operands are widened.
State that CMSIS-NN follows the LiteRT int8/int16 quantization spec and is bit-exact with the TFLM reference kernels, so it can replace them transparently.
Recall the TFLM paper's speed-up from optimized kernels: more than 4× for VWW on a Cortex-M4.
Build with CMSIS-NN kernels and compare latency against the reference kernels.
refs: Lai, Suda & Chandra, CMSIS-NN: Efficient Neural Network Kernels for Arm Cortex-M CPUs (arXiv 1801.06601, 2018)

units.title: Loop optimizations and MCU kernels
objectives: Apply loop reordering, tiling, unrolling and SIMD packing to a convolution or matrix-multiply loop nest.
Explain partial im2col on MCUs: unroll only a few columns at a time to bound the extra memory.
Explain in-place depthwise convolution: reuse the input buffer channel by channel to cut peak memory.
Explain why NHWC layout and operator fusion reduce memory traffic on MCUs.
keyTerms: memory hierarchy: register and SRAM reuse
refs: MIT 6.5940 Lecture 11: TinyEngine and Parallel Processing

units.title: TinyEngine and code generation
objectives: Contrast an interpreter (generic, reads the model at run time) with a code generator that emits model-specific code with memory planned at compile time.
Explain TinyEngine's model-adaptive memory scheduling and specialized kernels.
Recall MCUNet's figures for TinyEngine versus TF-Lite Micro and CMSIS-NN: 1.7–3.3× faster inference and 4.8× less memory.
Compare TinyEngine with Edge Impulse's EON Compiler as the same idea in an industrial tool.

units.title: Patch-based inference
objectives: Explain why the first few high-resolution layers set the peak memory of most CNNs.
Explain patch-based inference: run the memory-heavy first stage patch by patch so only one patch's activations are alive.
Compute the recomputation cost of overlapping receptive fields and explain how receptive-field redistribution limits it.
Recall MCUNetV2's results: 4–8× lower peak memory, 71.8% ImageNet top-1 on an MCU, and over 90% VWW accuracy within 32 KB of SRAM.

units.title: MicroNPUs and the Vela compiler
objectives: Explain microNPUs (Arm Ethos-U55, U65 and U85) as accelerators paired with a Cortex-M host.
Compile a quantized .tflite model with Vela: supported parts become an Ethos-U custom operator with a command stream, and unsupported parts are left for the CPU.
Use Vela's options (--accelerator-config, --system-config, --memory-mode, --optimise) and read its performance and memory report.
Explain why a few unsupported operators can erase the NPU's speed-up.

units.title: Capstone: keyword spotting on a Cortex-M board
objectives: Train a keyword spotter (micro_speech or Edge Impulse), quantize it to int8 and deploy it to a Cortex-M board such as the Arduino Nano 33 BLE Sense.
Measure flash use, arena size, per-inference latency and per-window processing time against the 20 ms stride budget.
Tune the detection threshold and averaging window on continuous audio to reach a target false-accept rate.
Compare reference kernels, CMSIS-NN kernels and an ahead-of-time compiled (EON) build on latency and memory.
refs: Banbury et al., MLPerf Tiny Benchmark, §4.3

modules.summary: Deploy models on phones and edge boards through the main runtimes, sending each part of the model to the CPU, GPU or NPU that can run it.

practice.title: ExecuTorch: getting started (export to .pte and run)

units.title: The edge-SoC landscape
objectives: Describe a heterogeneous SoC: big and little CPU cores, a GPU, DSPs and an NPU sharing DRAM.
Explain why the same model runs at very different speeds on CPU, GPU and NPU, and why thermal throttling lowers sustained performance.
Explain how uneven operator support across vendors' NPUs hurts portability.
Name milestones such as Apple's Neural Engine in the A11 chip (2017) and the spread of NPUs in phones.

units.title: LiteRT and delegates
objectives: Explain LiteRT (the successor to TensorFlow Lite): .tflite models run either through the Interpreter API with delegates or through the CompiledModel API with GPU and NPU acceleration.
Explain delegation: a delegate takes the subgraphs it supports and the rest runs on optimized CPU kernels.

Recall delegate limits: the GPU delegate runs fp32, fp16 and 8-bit models; the Core ML delegate needs an A12 or newer chip and runs float models only; a model type a delegate does not support runs entirely on the CPU.
Benchmark a model on the CPU versus the GPU delegate on a phone.

units.title: ExecuTorch and the .pte format
objectives: Trace the ExecuTorch flow: torch.export → Edge dialect → partition and lower to backends → .pte file → C++ runtime on the device.
Explain ahead-of-time memory planning in the .pte and why the runtime stays small.
List backends (XNNPACK, Core ML, Vulkan, Qualcomm, MediaTek, Arm Ethos-U, Arm Cortex-M and others) and how partitioners listed in priority order let unsupported operators fall back to the CPU.
Explain that ExecuTorch is PyTorch's on-device runtime, succeeding PyTorch Mobile.
Export a small model to .pte with the XNNPACK backend and run it.

units.title: ONNX Runtime and execution providers
objectives: Explain ONNX as a framework-neutral graph format with versioned opsets, and ONNX Runtime as an engine that runs it.
Explain execution providers (CPU, CUDA, TensorRT, OpenVINO, QNN, Core ML, XNNPACK and others) and how ONNX Runtime assigns nodes to providers in the priority order given.
Use graph-optimization levels and ONNX Runtime's quantization tools.
Run an exported model with a chosen provider list and verify the outputs.

units.title: Core ML and the Apple Neural Engine
objectives: Convert a PyTorch model to Core ML with coremltools (from a traced or exported model) into an ML Program package.
Choose compute units (CPU only, CPU and GPU, or all including the Neural Engine) and explain that the system decides the final placement.
Explain fp16 as Core ML's usual compute precision and its halving of model size versus fp32.
Explain why an operator the Neural Engine cannot run pushes part of the model onto the CPU or GPU.

units.title: TensorRT on Jetson
objectives: Explain TensorRT's build step: parse the network, fuse layers, pick the fastest kernels for the target GPU and serialize an engine.
Choose a precision (FP16, INT8 with calibration or explicit quantization, FP8 on newer GPUs) and measure the accuracy change.
Explain why an engine is tied to the GPU model and TensorRT version that built it, and how optimization profiles handle dynamic shapes.
Deploy an ONNX model to an NVIDIA Jetson with TensorRT and compare latency with ONNX Runtime.
refs: NVIDIA TensorRT docs: quick start guide

units.title: CPU fallback and choosing a runtime
objectives: Explain the cost of CPU fallback: graph partitions, tensor copies between processors and synchronization at every boundary.
Estimate end-to-end latency from per-partition times plus transfer costs, and decide when keeping everything on the CPU is faster.
Measure backend coverage (share of operators and of run time) and rewrite or replace unsupported operators.
Choose a runtime per target (LiteRT, ExecuTorch, ONNX Runtime, Core ML, TensorRT) from the model's source framework, the hardware and update needs.

modules.title: Benchmarking
modules.summary: Measure accuracy, latency and energy the way MLPerf does, and report results that others can trust and reproduce.
refs: Banbury et al., MLPerf Tiny Benchmark (arXiv 2106.07597, 2021)

practice.title: MLPerf Tiny benchmark repository (reference models, training and runner)

units.title: The MLPerf Tiny suite
objectives: List the four tasks with dataset, reference model and quality target: keyword spotting (Speech Commands v2, DS-CNN, 90% top-1), visual wake words (COCO-derived, MobileNetV1 0.25, 80%), image classification (CIFAR-10, small ResNet, 85%) and anomaly detection (ToyADMOS toy car, FC autoencoder, AUC 0.85).

Explain the closed division (same models and data; post-training quantization with the provided calibration data allowed; no retraining) versus the open division (changes allowed if documented; accuracy target not required).
Explain the modular design: submitters can optimize any layer of the stack while results stay comparable.
Run a reference model through the benchmark harness.

units.title: Latency and tail latency
objectives: Describe MLPerf Tiny latency: five runs, each at least 10 s and at least 10 inferences, scored as the median inferences per second.
Describe MLPerf Inference edge scenarios: single-stream (90th-percentile latency), multistream (99th-percentile latency, 8 samples per query) and offline (throughput).
Compute p50, p90 and p99 from a latency log and explain why tail latency matters for interactive devices.
List sources of variance on devices (clock scaling, caches, interrupts, temperature) and how to control them.

units.title: Energy and power measurement
objectives: Distinguish power (W) from energy per inference (µJ) and convert between them using latency.

Describe MLPerf Tiny's energy mode: an energy monitor (e.g., Joulescope JS110, STM LPM01A or Keysight N6705) measures core power only, an IO manager isolates the serial link, and the median of five runs is reported.
Define the measurement boundary (core, chip or board) and explain why results compare only within the same boundary.
Estimate battery life from energy per inference, inference rate and sleep power (duty cycling).
refs: Banbury et al. (2021), §5.3 and App. A

units.title: Benchmarking pitfalls and honest reporting
objectives: Spot pitfalls: reporting MACs instead of measured latency, model-only timing that hides pre-processing, cherry-picked runs and over-tuning to the benchmark.
Report reproducibly: hardware, clocks, compiler flags, runtime and model versions, and accuracy with confidence intervals.
Explain why MLPerf Tiny times only model inference, excluding pre- and post-processing, and what that leaves out for a real product.

tiers.name: ML systems: compilers, runtimes, accelerators
tiers.summary: You can make ML code run fast on CPUs, GPUs, NPUs and FPGAs: measure where time goes, compile and tune kernels, plan memory, and reason about how an accelerator moves data. You can split a model across a device's processors and predict the result before deploying.

modules.title: CPU performance engineering
modules.summary: You will be able to find where a program spends its time on a CPU and speed up ML kernels with vector instructions, cache-friendly loops and a well-structured matrix multiply.
refs: Hennessy, Patterson & Kozyrakis, Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach, 7th ed. (Dec 2025), ch. 1, 2, 4 and App. B, G
Bryant & O'Hallaron, Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective, 3rd ed., ch. 1, 5, 6 (§1.9.1, §5.7–5.9, §5.14, §6.6)
MIT 6.172 Performance Engineering of Software Systems (OCW, Fall 2018)
MIT 6.5930 reading list (Spring 2026): Kernel Computation lectures (CPU, Vectorization, Memory)

practice.title: How to Optimize GEMM: step-by-step tutorial
BLIS framework (study its micro-kernels)
CMSIS-NN int8 kernels for Cortex-M
MIT 6.172 Performance Engineering (OCW) projects

units.title: Amdahl's law and scaling laws
objectives: State Amdahl's law, S = 1 / ((1 − f) + f / k), and compute overall speedup when a fraction f of run time is sped up k-fold, including the limit 1 / (1 − f) as k grows without bound.
Apply Amdahl's law to accelerator offload: an NPU that runs 80% of a model's time 10× faster gives only about 3.6× end to end.
State Gustafson's law and explain when weak scaling (growing the problem with the machine) is the right lens instead of strong scaling.
Compute parallel efficiency (speedup ÷ cores) and explain how serial sections, synchronization and load imbalance cap it.
refs: Amdahl, AFIPS Spring Joint Computer Conference, 1967
Gustafson, Reevaluating Amdahl's Law, Communications of the ACM 31(5), 1988

units.title: Profiling and hardware performance counters
objectives: Contrast sampling profilers with instrumentation and pick one for a given question (hot spots versus exact call counts).
Use Linux perf (perf stat, perf record/report) to measure cycles, instructions, IPC, cache misses and branch misses for an inference kernel.
Read a flame graph to find the dominant call path of an inference run.
Apply top-down microarchitecture analysis (front-end bound, back-end bound, bad speculation, retiring) to decide whether to attack memory access or instruction count.
Avoid measurement errors: no warm-up runs, CPU frequency scaling, coarse timers, timing debug builds.
refs: Yasin, A Top-Down Method for Performance Analysis and Counters Architecture, ISPASS 2014
Gregg, The Flame Graph, Communications of the ACM 59(6), 2016

units.title: The roofline model in depth
objectives: Define operational intensity as FLOPs ÷ bytes moved from a chosen memory level and compute it for GEMV, GEMM and a 3×3 convolution.
Compute attainable performance = min(peak compute, intensity × bandwidth) and the ridge point = peak ÷ bandwidth for a given CPU.
Add ceilings (no SIMD, no FMA, L1/L2/DRAM bandwidth) and say which optimization lifts a kernel toward which ceiling.
Place batch-1 fully connected layers and LLM decode left of the ridge point and explain why they are memory-bound.
Explain why a roofline does not predict the latency of tiny kernels dominated by loop or launch overhead.
refs: Williams, Waterman & Patterson, Roofline, Communications of the ACM 52(4), 2009
Ilic, Pratas & Sousa, Cache-aware Roofline Model, IEEE Computer Architecture Letters, 2014

units.title: SIMD on Arm: Neon and Helium
objectives: Explain SIMD lanes and count lanes per register: a 128-bit Neon register holds 16 int8, 8 int16 or 4 fp32 values.
Write an int8 dot-product loop with Neon intrinsics using SDOT (int8 products summed into int32 lanes) and state what FEAT_DotProd and FEAT_I8MM (SMMLA) add.

Describe Helium, the M-Profile Vector Extension of Armv8.1-M (first core: Cortex-M55, announced 2020): 128-bit vectors on the FP register file, beat-wise execution and tail predication for loop remainders.
Explain why widening multiplies (int8 × int8 → int32) and saturating narrowing shape every quantized kernel.
Compare auto-vectorization, intrinsics, CMSIS-NN and hand-written assembly by effort, portability and speed.
refs: Hennessy, Patterson & Kozyrakis, CA:AQA 7e, ch. 4 (SIMD extensions)
Bryant & O'Hallaron, CS:APP 3e, web aside OPT:SIMD
Arm Helium (M-Profile Vector Extension) documentation, developer.arm.com

units.title: Scalable vectors and matrix extensions: RVV, SVE2 and SME2
objectives: Explain vector-length-agnostic programming: one binary runs on hardware with different vector lengths.
Write an RVV 1.0 strip-mined loop with vsetvli and explain SEW (element width) and LMUL (register grouping).
Describe SVE2 predicate registers and how they differ from Neon's fixed 128-bit width.
Describe SME/SME2: streaming SVE mode, the ZA tile storage and outer-product instructions, and why outer products suit matrix multiply.
Explain why libraries such as KleidiAI hide these ISA differences behind per-feature micro-kernels.
refs: Hennessy, Patterson & Kozyrakis, CA:AQA 7e, ch. 4 and App. G (vector processors)

units.title: Loop tiling and data locality
objectives: Explain temporal and spatial locality and read a memory mountain to estimate bandwidth at each cache level.
Reorder the loops of a naive matrix multiply (ijk → ikj) and predict the change in cache misses for row-major arrays.
Tile (block) loops so a tile's working set fits in L1 or L2, choosing the tile size from cache capacity.
Compute how tiling raises operational intensity and moves a kernel right on the roofline.
Compare NCHW and NHWC layouts and im2col for convolution on CPUs, including the extra memory im2col costs.
Explain transform-based convolution: Winograd F(2×2, 3×3) needs 16 multiplies instead of 36 per 2×2 output tile (2.25× fewer), at the cost of wider intermediate values that make int8 harder.
refs: Bryant & O'Hallaron, CS:APP 3e, §6.2, §6.6.1–6.6.3 and web aside MEM:BLOCKING
Lam, Rothberg & Wolf, The Cache Performance and Optimizations of Blocked Algorithms, ASPLOS 1991
Sze et al., ch. 4 (kernel computation: Toeplitz/im2col, tiling, transforms)
Lavin & Gray, Fast Algorithms for Convolutional Neural Networks, CVPR 2016

units.title: Anatomy of a fast GEMM
objectives: Describe the Goto/BLIS structure: five loops around a register-blocked micro-kernel, with packed panels of A and B sized for the caches (mc, kc, nc) and an mr × nr register tile.
Explain why packing copies data into contiguous, aligned panels and when its cost is amortized.
Compute flops per loaded element for an mr × nr micro-kernel and show why larger register tiles reach a higher fraction of peak.
Write the inner loop of an int8 GEMM that accumulates in int32 and requantizes to int8 with a fixed-point multiplier and shift, CMSIS-NN style.
Judge when to call a library (BLIS, XNNPACK, CMSIS-NN) and when to let a compiler generate the kernel.
refs: Goto & van de Geijn, Anatomy of High-Performance Matrix Multiplication, ACM TOMS 34(3), 2008
Van Zee & van de Geijn, BLIS: A Framework for Rapidly Instantiating BLAS Functionality, ACM TOMS 41(3), 2015
Hennessy, Patterson & Kozyrakis, CA:AQA 7e, ch. 2 and 4

modules.title: GPUs and parallel programming
modules.summary: You will be able to write and tune GPU kernels in CUDA and Triton by reasoning about warps, memory access patterns, occupancy and tensor cores.
refs: Hwu, Kirk & El Hajj, Programming Massively Parallel Processors, 4th ed. (2022), ch. 1–6, 10–11, 16, 20
NVIDIA CUDA Programming Guide and CUDA C++ Best Practices Guide (docs.nvidia.com/cuda)

practice.title: Triton tutorials: vector add, fused softmax, matrix multiplication
How to optimize a CUDA matmul kernel, step by step
CUDA Programming Guide
GPU MODE lecture series

units.title: GPU architecture and the SIMT model
objectives: Describe a GPU as many streaming multiprocessors (SMs), each running warps of 32 threads in lock-step (SIMT) under warp schedulers.
Explain latency hiding: an SM keeps many warps resident and switches to a ready warp on every stall instead of relying on big caches and out-of-order logic.
Explain branch divergence: both paths of a branch run with inactive lanes masked off.
Contrast latency-oriented CPU cores with throughput-oriented GPU cores by the chip area spent on control, cache and arithmetic.
Place the milestones: unified shader GPUs and CUDA (2006–2007) made GPUs general-purpose; Volta (2017) added tensor cores.
refs: Hwu, Kirk & El Hajj, PMPP 4e, ch. 1 and 4
Lindholm et al., NVIDIA Tesla: A Unified Graphics and Computing Architecture, IEEE Micro 28(2), 2008

units.title: The CUDA programming model
objectives: Write a CUDA kernel marked __global__, launch it with <<<grid, block>>>, and compute a global index from blockIdx, blockDim and threadIdx.
Manage host and device memory (cudaMalloc, cudaMemcpy, unified memory) and estimate the cost of host–device copies.
Use __syncthreads() correctly and explain why it must not sit inside divergent control flow.
Map a 2-D problem (an image or matrix) onto a 2-D grid of 2-D blocks, guarding boundary threads.
Overlap copies with kernels using CUDA streams.
refs: Hwu, Kirk & El Hajj, PMPP 4e, ch. 2, 3 and 20
Nickolls, Buck, Garland & Skadron, Scalable Parallel Programming with CUDA, ACM Queue 6(2), 2008

units.title: Memory coalescing and shared memory
objectives: Explain memory coalescing: when a warp's 32 threads touch consecutive addresses, the hardware merges them into a few wide transactions.
Rewrite a strided or column-wise access to be coalesced, for example by transposing through shared memory.
Implement a tiled matrix multiply in shared memory and show that tile width T cuts global-memory traffic by about a factor of T.
Explain shared-memory bank conflicts and the padding trick that removes them.
Order the GPU memory hierarchy (registers, shared memory/L1, L2, global memory) by capacity, latency and bandwidth.
refs: Hwu, Kirk & El Hajj, PMPP 4e, ch. 5 and 6
NVIDIA CUDA C++ Best Practices Guide

units.title: Occupancy and latency hiding
objectives: Define occupancy as active warps ÷ maximum warps per SM and compute it from registers per thread, shared memory per block and block size.
Use Little's law (work in flight = latency × throughput) to estimate how many bytes or warps must be in flight to saturate memory bandwidth.
Explain why higher occupancy is not always faster: instruction-level parallelism and register tiling can win at lower occupancy.
Diagnose a kernel limited by register spilling or by too few blocks for the number of SMs (tail effect).
refs: Hwu, Kirk & El Hajj, PMPP 4e, ch. 4 and 6
Volkov, Better Performance at Lower Occupancy, NVIDIA GTC 2010
Little, A Proof for the Queuing Formula L = λW, Operations Research 9(3), 1961

units.title: Reduction and scan patterns
objectives: Implement a tree reduction in shared memory and rearrange it to minimize warp divergence.
Finish a reduction with warp shuffles (__shfl_down_sync) instead of shared memory.
Explain inclusive versus exclusive prefix sums and the work-efficient (Brent–Kung) scan.
Implement a numerically safe softmax as two reductions (maximum, then sum of exponentials).
refs: Hwu, Kirk & El Hajj, PMPP 4e, ch. 10 and 11

units.title: Tensor cores and hierarchical GEMM tiling
objectives: Explain what a tensor core does: a small matrix multiply-accumulate per instruction (for example FP16 or BF16 inputs with FP32 accumulation) issued by a whole warp.
Describe the CUTLASS hierarchy of thread-block tiles, warp tiles and instruction (MMA) tiles, and why each level stages data in a faster memory.
Compute a thread-block tile's arithmetic intensity and decide whether a GEMM shape is tensor-core-bound or memory-bound on a hierarchical roofline.
Explain why tensor-core peak far exceeds CUDA-core peak and what that implies for unfused elementwise work (Amdahl again).
Choose among FP16, BF16, TF32, FP8 and INT8 inputs by range, precision and throughput.
refs: Hwu, Kirk & El Hajj, PMPP 4e, ch. 16 (Deep learning)
NVIDIA Tesla V100 (Volta) GPU architecture whitepaper, 2017

units.title: Triton and IO-aware fused kernels
objectives: Write a Triton kernel in which each program instance handles one block, using tl.program_id, tl.arange and masked tl.load/tl.store, and launch it over a grid.
Fuse softmax into one kernel and compute the global-memory traffic saved versus separate max, exp, sum and divide kernels.
Explain FlashAttention: tile Q, K and V through on-chip SRAM with an online (running) softmax so the N × N attention matrix never reaches HBM.
Use Triton's autotuner to choose block sizes and warp counts, and say what Triton automates compared with CUDA (shared-memory staging, coalescing).
refs: Tillet, Kung & Cox, Triton: An Intermediate Language and Compiler for Tiled Neural Network Computations, MAPL 2019
Triton tutorials (triton-lang.org): fused softmax, matrix multiplication
Milakov & Gimelshein, Online normalizer calculation for softmax, arXiv:1805.02867, 2018

modules.title: Framework internals
modules.summary: You will be able to explain what a PyTorch-style framework does between a line of model code and a running kernel, and how trained models are saved for deployment.
refs: Janapa Reddi et al., Machine Learning Systems (mlsysbook.ai) Vol. I, ch. 7 (ML Frameworks)

practice.title: CMU Deep Learning Systems assignments: build the needle framework
MiniTorch: build a tensor library with autodiff
micrograd: a tiny autograd engine

units.title: Eager execution and graph capture
objectives: Contrast eager (define-by-run) with graph (define-then-run) execution in debuggability, optimization scope and deployability.
Explain how torch.compile captures graphs with TorchDynamo (Python bytecode analysis) and what causes a graph break.
Use torch.export to produce one whole, static graph for ahead-of-time deployment and state what it rejects (untraced data-dependent control flow).
Explain static versus dynamic shapes and why shape specialization and recompilation matter on devices.
refs: Ansel et al., PyTorch 2: Faster Machine Learning Through Dynamic Python Bytecode Transformation and Graph Compilation, ASPLOS 2024
Janapa Reddi et al., mlsysbook.ai Vol. I, ch. 7
CMU DLSys lecture 7 (Neural Network Library Abstractions)

units.title: Inside an autograd engine
objectives: Explain reverse-mode automatic differentiation as vector–Jacobian products propagated backward over a topologically sorted graph.
Implement a minimal autograd: tensors record parents and a backward function; backward() walks the graph in reverse topological order and accumulates gradients.
Compute the activations a small MLP must save for backward and explain why training needs far more memory than inference.
Explain gradient checkpointing (recompute activations instead of storing them) and its compute–memory trade-off.
refs: CMU DLSys lectures 4–5 (Automatic Differentiation and its implementation)
Baydin et al., Automatic Differentiation in Machine Learning: a Survey, JMLR 18, 2018
Chen et al., Training Deep Nets with Sublinear Memory Cost, arXiv:1604.06174, 2016

units.title: Tensors, views and operator dispatch
objectives: Explain a tensor as storage plus sizes, strides and offset, and predict which operations return views (transpose, slice) and which copy.
Explain dispatch: one operator call is routed by dispatch keys (device, autograd, quantized, functionalization) to a backend kernel.
Register a custom operator with a CPU kernel and a meta (fake) implementation so that graph capture and export work.
Estimate per-operator framework overhead and explain why many tiny ops are slow in eager mode.

units.title: Framework memory allocators
objectives: Explain why frameworks use caching allocators instead of calling malloc or cudaMalloc for every tensor.
Describe internal and external fragmentation and read allocator statistics (allocated versus reserved memory).
Contrast dynamic caching allocators on servers with static arenas planned ahead of time on microcontrollers.
Debug an out-of-memory error by finding which tensors are alive at the peak.
refs: PyTorch documentation, CUDA semantics: memory management
Janapa Reddi et al., mlsysbook.ai Vol. I, ch. 7

units.title: Model serialization formats
objectives: Compare ONNX (protobuf graph with versioned opsets), LiteRT/TFLite (.tflite FlatBuffer), ExecuTorch (.pte), GGUF and safetensors by what they store and how they load.
Explain why FlatBuffers allow zero-copy, memory-mapped loading on devices while protobuf must be parsed.
Explain opset versioning and why a model can fail to load on an older runtime.
Place the landmarks: ONNX (2017); TensorFlow Lite renamed LiteRT on 4 Sep 2024 with the .tflite format unchanged; ExecuTorch 1.0 (Oct 2025); GGUF replacing the GGML/GGMF/GGJT formats.
refs: Google AI Edge Team, TensorFlow Lite is now LiteRT, Google Developers Blog, 4 Sep 2024
PyTorch, Introducing ExecuTorch 1.0, PyTorch blog, Oct 2025

modules.title: ML compilers
modules.summary: You will be able to explain how ML compilers turn a model graph into fast code for a specific device, and use TVM, MLIR-based tools, XLA, IREE and ExecuTorch.
refs: Chen et al., Machine Learning Compilation course notes (mlc.ai, 2022), ch. 1–7
Chen et al., TVM: An Automated End-to-End Optimizing Compiler for Deep Learning, OSDI 2018
Lattner et al., MLIR: Scaling Compiler Infrastructure for Domain Specific Computation, CGO 2021
Stanford CS217 (Winter 2026), Compilers and software stack lectures (parts 1–2)

practice.title: MLC course (2022): episodes, notebooks and exercises
Apache TVM documentation (Relax, TensorIR, MetaSchedule)
Halide tutorials
IREE: MLIR-based compiler and runtime

units.title: Why ML compilers: IR levels and lowering
objectives: Explain the deployment problem (many models × many hardware targets) and why hand-written kernel libraries do not scale to new operators and fused patterns.
Distinguish graph-level IR (operators on tensors), tensor-level IR (loops and buffers) and hardware-level IR (LLVM IR, SPIR-V, assembly) and what is optimized at each.
Name current IRs at each level: Relax and TensorIR (TVM), StableHLO and HLO (XLA), MLIR linalg/tensor/memref, the Edge dialect (ExecuTorch).
Explain lowering as a sequence of progressively more hardware-specific representations.
refs: mlc.ai, ch. 1 (Introduction) and ch. 2 (Tensor Program Abstraction)
Apache TVM documentation (tvm.apache.org/docs): Relax and TensorIR

units.title: Graph optimizations and operator fusion
objectives: Apply constant folding, dead-code elimination, common-subexpression elimination and algebraic simplification to a small graph.
Classify operators for fusion (injective, reduction, complex-out-fusable such as conv2d, opaque) and decide which neighbours can fuse.
Compute the memory traffic saved by fusing conv → batch-norm → ReLU (fold batch norm into the weights, apply ReLU in the epilogue).
Explain when fusion hurts: register pressure, losing a tuned library kernel, recomputation.
refs: Chen et al., TVM, OSDI 2018 (graph-level optimizations)
Jia et al., TASO: Optimizing Deep Learning Computation with Automatic Generation of Graph Substitutions, SOSP 2019

units.title: Data layouts and layout transformation
objectives: Compare NCHW, NHWC and blocked NCHWc layouts for SIMD CPUs, GPUs and NPUs.
Insert and eliminate layout transforms in a graph and compute the cost of a transpose for a given tensor.
Explain weight pre-packing at compile time and why it removes runtime transforms.
Choose layouts that match a target's vector width or tensor-core tile shape.
refs: Liu et al., Optimizing CNN Model Inference on CPUs (NeoCPU), USENIX ATC 2019

units.title: Halide: separating algorithm from schedule
objectives: Explain Halide's split between what to compute (the algorithm) and how to compute it (the schedule), and why one algorithm can then target many machines.
Apply split, reorder, tile, vectorize, parallel, compute_at and store_at to a two-stage blur and predict the effect on locality and recomputation.
Describe the three-way trade-off among parallelism, locality and redundant recomputation.
Explain how TVM adopted Halide-style schedules for deep learning operators.
refs: Ragan-Kelley et al., Halide: A Language and Compiler for Optimizing Parallelism, Locality, and Recomputation in Image Processing Pipelines, PLDI 2013

units.title: Tensor programs in TensorIR
objectives: Read a TensorIR function: buffers, loop nests and blocks with spatial and reduction iterators.
Transform a matmul with split, reorder, cache_read/cache_write and thread binding for a GPU, checking correctness after each step.
Use tensorize to map an inner loop nest onto a hardware intrinsic such as a dot-product or MMA instruction.
Explain why schedule primitives are semantics-preserving program transformations.
refs: mlc.ai, ch. 2 (Tensor Program Abstraction) and ch. 6 (GPU and Hardware Acceleration)
Feng et al., TensorIR: An Abstraction for Automatic Tensorized Program Optimization, ASPLOS 2023

units.title: Autotuning: AutoTVM, Ansor and MetaSchedule
objectives: Explain the search problem: a space of tiling factors, loop orders and bindings, scored by measuring candidates on hardware.
Contrast template-based AutoTVM with Ansor's template-free hierarchical search (sketches, random annotation, evolutionary search guided by a learned cost model).
Explain how a learned cost model (for example gradient-boosted trees on loop features) cuts the number of on-device measurements.
Weigh tuning time (often hours per model) against speedup, and reuse tuning logs across models and devices.
refs: Chen et al., Learning to Optimize Tensor Programs, NeurIPS 2018
Zheng et al., Ansor: Generating High-Performance Tensor Programs for Deep Learning, OSDI 2020
Shao et al., Tensor Program Optimization with Probabilistic Programs (MetaSchedule), NeurIPS 2022

units.title: MLIR: dialects, linalg and TOSA
objectives: Explain MLIR's core ideas: operations with regions and blocks, dialects as extensible operation sets, and progressive lowering between dialects.
Read a linalg.generic op (indexing maps, iterator types) and explain why structured ops make tiling and fusion generic.
Explain tensor versus memref types and the role of bufferization.
Describe TOSA as a frontend-neutral, hardware-oriented operator set (the contract used by Arm's Ethos-U backends) and StableHLO as the XLA ecosystem's portable operator set.

units.title: XLA and StableHLO
objectives: Trace XLA's flow: trace a function (jax.jit or tf.function) → StableHLO → HLO optimizations (fusion, layout assignment) → backend code.
Explain why XLA specializes on static shapes and what triggers recompilation.
Contrast XLA's whole-program fusion with eager, kernel-by-kernel execution.

units.title: Ahead-of-time compilation for devices: IREE and ExecuTorch
objectives: Describe IREE: an MLIR-based compiler plus a small runtime with a hardware abstraction layer (HAL), targeting CPUs through LLVM, GPUs through Vulkan/SPIR-V or CUDA, and bare-metal builds.
Trace the ExecuTorch flow torch.export → to_edge (Edge dialect) → to_backend (partition and delegate) → .pte file, run by the C++ runtime.
Contrast an interpreter with per-operator kernels (TensorFlow Lite Micro) and an AOT-compiled module by binary size, flexibility and speed.
Locate where memory planning and backend delegation happen in these pipelines.
refs: ExecuTorch documentation: export, lowering and backend delegation (docs.pytorch.org/executorch)

units.title: End-to-end compile, measure and verify
objectives: Compile one model with two flows (for example TVM, and ExecuTorch with XNNPACK) and compare latency, binary size and peak memory on the same device.
Verify numerical equivalence against the eager reference with per-layer tolerances and localize a mismatch to a single operator.
Decide when a vendor library beats compiler-generated code and how to combine the two.
refs: mlc.ai, ch. 3 (End-to-End Model Execution) and ch. 5 (Integration with Machine Learning Frameworks)

modules.summary: You will be able to fit a model's working memory into a small RAM by planning when each tensor lives, where it is stored and how data streams in.

Lin et al., MCUNetV2: Memory-Efficient Patch-based Inference for Tiny Deep Learning, NeurIPS 2021
