ExecuTorch memory planning documentation
TensorFlow Lite Micro (study the arena planner)

units.title: Tensor liveness and peak memory
objectives: Compute each activation tensor's live interval from the execution order and find the peak of simultaneously live bytes.
Explain why on microcontrollers weights stay in flash while activations must fit in SRAM, so peak activation memory, not model size, often decides feasibility.
Show for a MobileNetV2-style network that the first blocks dominate peak memory (an imbalanced memory distribution).
Distinguish peak memory from total allocated memory and from parameter count.
refs: MIT 6.5940 (Fall 2024), L10 MCUNet: TinyML on Microcontrollers

units.title: Arena packing and static memory planners
objectives: Formulate static memory planning as assigning offsets in one arena so that tensors with overlapping lifetimes never overlap in address (a 2-D packing problem).
Run the greedy-by-size and greedy-by-breadth heuristics by hand and compare the arena size with the lower bound (maximum live bytes).
Explain how TensorFlow Lite Micro's tensor arena and ExecuTorch's memory-planning pass assign offsets at build time.
Explain why optimal packing is NP-hard and heuristics are used in practice.
refs: Pisarchyk & Lee, Efficient Memory Management for Deep Neural Net Inference, arXiv:2001.03288, 2020

units.title: Operator reordering and in-place execution
objectives: Show that in a branching network the order of independent operators changes peak memory, and find a better order by hand.
Explain how SERENITY searches execution orders with dynamic programming to minimize peak memory of irregularly wired networks.
Identify operators that can run in place (ReLU, residual add, TinyEngine's in-place depthwise convolution) and the aliasing conditions that forbid it.
Weigh reordering against latency and cache behaviour.
refs: Ahn et al., Ordering Chaos: Memory-Aware Scheduling of Irregularly Wired Neural Networks for Edge Devices (SERENITY), MLSys 2020
MIT 6.5940 (Fall 2024 and Fall 2026), L11 TinyEngine and Parallel Processing

units.title: Patch-based inference
objectives: Explain MCUNetV2's patch-by-patch execution of the memory-heavy first stage and why it cuts peak memory of existing networks by 4–8×.
Compute the receptive-field overlap between neighbouring patches and the resulting recomputation overhead.
Explain receptive-field redistribution (shift receptive field and FLOPs to later stages) and the joint search of architecture and inference schedule.
Decide when patch-based inference is worth its extra compute (SRAM-bound MCU) and when it is not.

units.title: Double buffering and DMA overlap
objectives: Implement ping-pong (double) buffering so a DMA engine loads tile i + 1 while the core computes tile i.
Estimate time per tile as max(compute, transfer) with overlap versus compute + transfer without, and find the tile size at which transfer stops dominating.
Stream weights from external flash or PSRAM in tiles when they do not fit in SRAM.
Explain decoupled data orchestration (buffets) in accelerators as the hardware form of the same idea.
refs: Pellauer et al., Buffets: An Efficient and Composable Storage Idiom for Explicit Decoupled Data Orchestration, ASPLOS 2019
Hwu, Kirk & El Hajj, PMPP 4e, ch. 20 (CUDA streams)

modules.title: Accelerator fundamentals
modules.summary: You will be able to explain why custom ML chips beat general-purpose processors and how their compute arrays, on-chip memories and interconnects are built.
refs: Sze, Chen, Yang & Emer, Efficient Processing of Deep Neural Networks (2020), ch. 1, 3, 5 and 7
Jouppi et al., In-Datacenter Performance Analysis of a Tensor Processing Unit, ISCA 2017
Hennessy, Patterson & Kozyrakis, CA:AQA 7e, ch. 7 (Domain-Specific Architectures)
Stanford CS217 Hardware Accelerators for Machine Learning (Winter 2026): systolic arrays, vector and scalar units, memory systems, interconnects
MIT 6.5930/1 Hardware Architecture for Deep Learning (Spring 2026 reading list): Accelerator Architecture

practice.title: SCALE-Sim v3 systolic-array simulator
Gemmini systolic-array generator

units.title: Why domain-specific accelerators
objectives: Explain how the end of Dennard scaling and slowing Moore's law pushed architects toward specialization.
Use Horowitz's 45 nm energy table to show data movement dominates: a 32-bit DRAM read (~640 pJ) costs ~6,400× a 32-bit integer add (~0.1 pJ) and ~128× a 32-bit read from an 8 KB SRAM (~5 pJ).
List the sources of accelerator efficiency: massive parallelism, data reuse in local memories, reduced precision and removal of instruction overheads.
Correct the misconception that accelerators win mainly through faster arithmetic units.
refs: Horowitz, Computing's Energy Problem (and What We Can Do About It), ISSCC 2014
Hennessy & Patterson, A New Golden Age for Computer Architecture, Communications of the ACM 62(2), 2019

units.title: Metrics for accelerators
objectives: Compute peak throughput as 2 × (number of MACs) × clock frequency, for example 2048 MACs at 1 GHz ≈ 4 TOPS.
Define utilization, TOPS/W, TOPS/mm², latency, throughput and energy per inference, and explain why peak TOPS alone is a weak metric.
Explain how batch size trades latency for utilization and why edge inference usually runs at batch 1.
List what a fair comparison must report: precision, workload, achieved utilization, and whether off-chip memory energy is included.
refs: Sze, Chen, Yang & Emer, How to Evaluate Deep Neural Network Processors, IEEE Solid-State Circuits Magazine 12(3), 2020
Stanford CS217 (Winter 2026), Data Parallelism and Efficiency Metrics lecture

units.title: Systolic arrays
objectives: Explain Kung's systolic idea: data pulses through a grid of simple processing elements, each reusing operands passed from neighbours instead of re-reading memory.
Trace a weight-stationary 2-D systolic matrix multiply cycle by cycle, including the skewing of inputs.
Compute the fill and drain overhead (about R + C extra cycles for an R × C array) and utilization when the matrix is smaller than the array.
Use a simulator such as SCALE-Sim to compare array shapes (for example 32 × 32 versus 128 × 128) for one layer.
refs: Kung, Why Systolic Architectures?, IEEE Computer 15(1), 1982
Samajdar et al., A Systematic Methodology for Characterizing Scalability of DNN Accelerators using SCALE-Sim, ISPASS 2020

units.title: Case study: TPU v1
objectives: Describe TPU v1: a 256 × 256 array of 65,536 8-bit MACs at 700 MHz giving 92 TOPS peak, 28 MiB of software-managed on-chip memory (24 MiB unified buffer + 4 MiB accumulators), and weights streamed from 8 GiB of DDR3 at 34 GB/s.
Use the paper's roofline to explain why MLPs and LSTMs were limited by weight-memory bandwidth while CNNs were compute-bound.
Explain why the TPU targeted 99th-percentile latency and why it omitted caches, branch prediction and multithreading.
Quote the headline result (about 15–30× faster and 30–80× higher TOPS/W than contemporary CPU and GPU) and say what such a comparison does and does not show.
refs: Jouppi et al., In-Datacenter Performance Analysis of a Tensor Processing Unit, ISCA 2017

units.title: Processing element design
objectives: Explain why multiplier area and energy grow roughly with the square of operand width, making 8-bit MACs far cheaper than 32-bit floating-point ones.
Size an accumulator: an int8 × int8 product needs 16 bits and summing K products needs about log2(K) more, hence int32 accumulators.
Describe what a PE holds locally (small register file, partial sums) and why local storage saves energy.
Compare fixed-precision MACs with precision-scalable designs (bit-serial units, Bit Fusion-style composable units).

Explain why accelerators pair the MAC array with vector and scalar units (activations, normalization, softmax, control) and how an under-sized vector unit becomes an Amdahl bottleneck for transformers.
refs: Sze et al., ch. 5 and ch. 7
Camus et al., Review and Benchmarking of Precision-Scalable Multiply-Accumulate Unit Architectures for Embedded Neural-Network Processing, IEEE JETCAS 2019
Sharma et al., Bit Fusion, ISCA 2018

units.title: Scratchpads and on-chip buffers
objectives: Contrast hardware-managed caches with software-managed scratchpads (explicit data orchestration) for the predictable access patterns of DNNs.

Lay out a typical accelerator memory hierarchy (DRAM → global buffer → inter-PE network → PE register file) and its Eyeriss-style normalized energy per access (DRAM ≈ 200×, global buffer ≈ 6×, neighbouring PE ≈ 2×, register file ≈ 1×).
Explain banking, double buffering and the buffet idiom (fill, read, update, shrink) for decoupling data movement from compute.
Size a global buffer so a layer tile fits, and compute DRAM traffic when it does not.
refs: Chen, Emer & Sze, Eyeriss: A Spatial Architecture for Energy-Efficient Dataflow for CNNs, ISCA 2016

units.title: On-chip networks for accelerators
objectives: Compare bus, crossbar, mesh and tree networks by bandwidth, latency, area and support for broadcast.
Explain why DNN accelerators need multicast (one weight or activation to many PEs) and reduction (partial sums to one place), and how the Eyeriss NoC provides them.
Describe MAERI's reconfigurable distribution and reduction trees and why flexible interconnect helps irregular layer shapes.
Introduce collective patterns (broadcast, reduce, all-reduce) that return when scaling across chips.
refs: Chen et al., Eyeriss: An Energy-Efficient Reconfigurable Accelerator for Deep Convolutional Neural Networks, IEEE JSSC 52(1), 2017
Stanford CS217 (Winter 2026), Interconnects and network-on-chip lecture

units.title: The hardware–software interface of accelerators
objectives: Describe how a host drives an accelerator: memory-mapped control registers, command queues and descriptors, interrupts and DMA.
Explain TPU v1's CISC-style instructions sent over PCIe (Read_Host_Memory, Read_Weights, MatrixMultiply/Convolve, Activate, Write_Host_Memory).
Explain RoCC custom instructions in Gemmini as a tightly coupled alternative to memory-mapped offload.
Compute when offload overhead (setup plus transfers) outweighs the speedup for a small layer.
refs: Genc et al., Gemmini: Enabling Systematic Deep-Learning Architecture Evaluation via Full-Stack Integration, DAC 2021

modules.title: Dataflow and mapping
modules.summary: You will be able to describe any layer as a loop nest, reason about how a chip reuses data, and search for the schedule that minimizes energy and time, using Timeloop.
refs: MIT 6.5930/1 Hardware Architecture for Deep Learning (Spring 2026), L03–L07, L13 and recitations (AccelForge tutorial, looptree)
Parashar et al., Timeloop: A Systematic Approach to DNN Accelerator Evaluation, ISPASS 2019

units.title: Loop nests and Einsums
objectives: Write a convolution layer as a 7-deep loop nest over N, M, C, P, Q, R, S and count its MACs as the product of the loop bounds.
Express matmul, convolution and the attention products (QKᵀ and AV) as Einsums with named ranks, and say which ranks index each tensor.
Identify reduction ranks versus output ranks and explain why reduction ranks create partial sums.
Compute MACs and tensor sizes for a transformer block from its Einsums.
refs: MIT 6.5930 recitation: Writing Mappings in Python (Lab 2)

units.title: Data reuse
objectives: Define convolutional reuse, filter (weight) reuse and input-feature-map reuse, and count the reuse available for each tensor of a given layer.
Distinguish temporal reuse (same PE, later cycle) from spatial reuse (one fetch multicast to many PEs).
Compute the algorithmic minimum DRAM traffic for a layer and compare it with a naive schedule.
Relate per-tensor reuse to operational intensity and the roofline.

units.title: Weight-, output- and row-stationary dataflows
objectives: Define weight-stationary, output-stationary, input-stationary and no-local-reuse dataflows by which operand stays in each PE, with an example chip for each (TPU, ShiDianNao, DianNao).
Explain Eyeriss's row-stationary dataflow: each PE runs a 1-D row convolution so all three data types are reused in its register file.
Compare dataflows by energy breakdown (DRAM, buffer, array, register file) using the Eyeriss analysis.
Show that a dataflow is a choice of loop order plus spatial unrolling.

units.title: Representing mappings
objectives: Define a mapping as the tiling factors, loop order and spatial/temporal assignment of every rank at every memory level.
Write a mapping as a multi-level loop nest and check it against buffer capacities and the number of PEs.
Compute the PE utilization lost when loop bounds do not divide evenly by the array dimensions.
Read MAESTRO's data-centric directives as an alternative notation.
refs: Kwon et al., Understanding Reuse, Performance, and Hardware Cost of DNN Dataflows: A Data-Centric Approach (MAESTRO), MICRO 2019
MIT 6.5930 (Spring 2026), L03 Mapping: Dataflow & Partitioning and L05 Mapping

units.title: Analytical cost models
objectives: Count accesses to each memory level for each tensor from a mapping's tile sizes and loop order.
Compute energy as the sum of (accesses × energy per access) using Accelergy-style tables, and latency as the maximum of compute cycles and each level's bandwidth-limited cycles.
Explain where analytical models lose accuracy (control overheads, bank conflicts, network contention) and how they are validated against RTL or silicon.
refs: Wu, Emer & Sze, Accelergy: An Architecture-Level Energy Estimation Methodology for Accelerator Designs, ICCAD 2019
MIT 6.5930 (Spring 2026), L13 Computing Data Movement in ISL

units.title: Searching the mapspace
objectives: Estimate the mapspace size for a layer and explain why exhaustive search is infeasible.
Compare search methods: pruned random sampling (Timeloop mapper), heuristics, genetic search (GAMMA), gradient-based surrogates (Mind Mappings) and mixed-integer programming (CoSA).
Trade search time against mapping quality and explain how designer-supplied constraints shrink the space.
refs: Kao & Krishna, GAMMA: Automating the HW Mapping of DNN Models on Accelerators via Genetic Algorithm, ICCAD 2020
Hegde et al., Mind Mappings, ASPLOS 2021
Huang et al., CoSA: Scheduling by Constrained Optimization for Spatial Accelerators, ISCA 2021

units.title: Hands-on: Timeloop, Accelergy and AccelForge
objectives: Write Timeloop inputs (architecture, problem/workload and mapper/constraint specifications in YAML) for one conv layer on an Eyeriss-like architecture.
Run the mapper and read the outputs: energy per MAC by component, utilization, cycles and the chosen mapping.
Change one architectural parameter (global buffer size or PE count) and explain the change in energy and cycles.
Describe AccelForge, the newer framework from the same group (used in MIT 6.5930 in 2026): it adds fusion modelling and a faster constraint-free mapper, with HWComponents replacing Accelergy.
refs: Andrulis et al., AccelForge: Comprehensive Modeling and Co-Design Framework for AI Accelerators, arXiv:2609.11906, 2026

units.title: Layer fusion dataflows
objectives: Explain fused-layer execution: compute a tile of layer i + 1 from a tile of layer i so the intermediate never goes to DRAM.
Compute the DRAM traffic saved and the recompute or buffer cost of fusing two convolutions (tile-and-recompute versus tile-and-cache).
Describe LoopTree-style modelling of fused mappings and FlashAttention as fusion of the attention Einsums.
Decide when fusion pays off given the on-chip buffer capacity.
refs: Alwani et al., Fused-Layer CNN Accelerators, MICRO 2016

units.title: Mapping transformers: prefill versus decode
objectives: Map the attention and feed-forward Einsums of a transformer layer and compute their operational intensity for prefill (many tokens: matrix–matrix) and decode (one token: matrix–vector).
Explain why batch-1 decode has almost no weight reuse and is bound by weight and KV-cache bandwidth.
Choose dataflows and buffer allocations that suit each phase and explain why a large array sits mostly idle during decode.
refs: Pope et al., Efficiently Scaling Transformer Inference, MLSys 2023
Stanford CS217 (Winter 2026), HW1: analytical modeling of LLM arithmetic performance

units.title: How NPUs fit into a system
objectives: Describe a microNPU system: Cortex-M host, NPU, shared SRAM and external flash, with the NPU executing a precompiled command stream.
Explain operator coverage: supported operators run on the NPU, the rest fall back to the CPU, and each switch costs synchronization and data movement.
Contrast fixed-function NPUs (fast, narrow operator set) with programmable DSP-like accelerators (slower, flexible).
Explain why the offline NPU compiler (Vela, ST Edge AI) is effectively part of the hardware product.

Run Vela on an int8 .tflite model and read its report: which operators map to the NPU, SRAM use and estimated cycles.
Explain Vela's weight compression and why compressed weights cut flash bandwidth.

objectives: State the STM32N6 figures from ST's 10 Dec 2024 announcement: 800 MHz Cortex-M55 (3,360 CoreMark), Neural-ART Accelerator with nearly 300 configurable MAC units reaching up to 600 GOPS, 4.2 MB of on-chip RAM, two 64-bit AXI interfaces.
Check 600 GOPS as 2 × ~300 MACs × 1 GHz, and explain why ST's '600× a high-end STM32' claim compares peak with peak.
Describe the ST Edge AI flow: quantized model → ST Edge AI Core / STM32Cube.AI → generated C code and NPU program, benchmarked on boards through the Developer Cloud.
Explain how external flash or PSRAM bandwidth limits throughput for models that do not fit on chip.
refs: STMicroelectronics press release P4665, STMicroelectronics to boost AI at the edge with new NPU-accelerated STM32 microcontrollers, 10 Dec 2024
ST Edge AI Developer Cloud documentation (stedgeai-dc.st.com)

units.title: NPUs in phones and laptops
objectives: Describe a heterogeneous mobile SoC (CPU clusters, GPU, DSP/NPU) and how runtimes choose a delegate for each subgraph.

Describe the Qualcomm Hexagon NPU path (QNN / AI Engine Direct; the ExecuTorch Qualcomm delegate, production-ready in ExecuTorch 1.0) and the Apple Neural Engine path (Core ML; the M4 Neural Engine is rated at 38 trillion operations per second, May 2024).
Explain why the same model can be fastest on the GPU of one phone and on the NPU of another (operator coverage, precision, memory placement).
Interpret vendor TOPS across generations without assuming the same precision or workload.

units.title: Edge TPU and int8-only accelerators
objectives: State the Edge TPU figures from the Coral USB Accelerator datasheet: 4 TOPS peak at int8 and 2 TOPS per watt.
Explain the full-integer requirement: every operator must be int8-quantized and compiled, and unsupported operators split the model and run on the host CPU.
Correct the misconception that a 4-TOPS accelerator runs any model four times faster than a 1-TOPS one.
Weigh a USB or PCIe accelerator against an integrated NPU (transfer overhead, power, cost).

units.title: Peak TOPS versus real utilization
objectives: Compute utilization = achieved operations per second ÷ peak, from a measured latency and a layer's MAC count.
List why utilization collapses at the edge: batch 1, depthwise and small layers that cannot fill the array, unsupported operators, external-memory bandwidth, and peak figures inflated by sparsity.
Build a roofline for an NPU (peak TOPS, on-chip and external bandwidth) and place each layer on it.
Treat vendor utilization claims (for example Arm's 'up to 85% utilization on popular networks' for Ethos-U85) as claims to test, and use MLPerf results for comparisons.

Use arbitrary-precision types (ap_int, ap_fixed) to shrink datapaths and estimate the resource savings.
Trade unroll factor against DSP and BRAM use to meet a throughput target.

Correct the misconception that streaming always wins: it fails once the weights exceed on-chip memory.
Place coarse-grained reconfigurable dataflow architectures (Plasticine; SambaNova's reconfigurable dataflow unit) between bit-level FPGAs and fixed ASICs.

objectives: Classify misses with the 3C model (compulsory, capacity, conflict) plus coherence misses (the fourth C) and explain how each arises.

Match techniques to miss types: larger blocks and prefetching (compulsory), larger caches (capacity), associativity and victim caches (conflict), protocol and data-layout changes (coherence).
Explain non-blocking caches with MSHRs and why memory-level parallelism matters to out-of-order cores.

Hill & Smith, Evaluating Associativity in CPU Caches, IEEE Transactions on Computers 38(12), 1989
Wisconsin CA qualifier, Fall 2020, Q1 (data caches)

units.title: Out-of-order execution and the reorder buffer
objectives: Explain register renaming (rename table, physical register file, free list) and how it removes WAR and WAW hazards.
Trace instructions through dispatch, issue queue, execute, writeback and in-order commit from the reorder buffer.
Explain how the ROB provides precise exceptions and recovery from branch mispredictions.
Explain the load–store queue, store-to-load forwarding and memory-dependence prediction.
Place Tomasulo's algorithm (IBM 360/91, 1967) and the reorder buffer (Smith & Pleszkun, 1985) in history.
refs: Tomasulo, An Efficient Algorithm for Exploiting Multiple Arithmetic Units, IBM Journal of R&D 11(1), 1967
Smith & Pleszkun, Implementation of Precise Interrupts in Pipelined Processors, ISCA 1985

units.title: Designing large instruction windows
objectives: List the subsystems that must scale for an 8-wide core with a ~1000-instruction window: fetch and branch prediction, rename, issue-queue wakeup and select, register-file ports, load–store queue, ROB and memory-level parallelism.
Explain why wakeup–select and register-file access form critical timing loops and how designs pipeline or partition them.
Describe checkpointing and runahead execution as alternatives to brute-force window growth.
Explain how the decisions interact, e.g. a larger window only pays off with better branch prediction and more MSHRs.
refs: Mutlu, Stark, Wilkerson & Patt, Runahead Execution, HPCA 2003
Wisconsin CA qualifier, Fall 2020, Q6 (out-of-order processor design)

units.title: Branch prediction and predication
objectives: Explain 2-bit saturating counters, local and global history, gshare and tournament predictors, plus the branch target buffer and return-address stack.
Describe TAGE (tagged geometric history lengths) and perceptron predictors as the modern state of the art.
Compute CPI lost to branches = branch frequency × misprediction rate × penalty, and the gain from a better predictor on a deeper pipeline.
Argue predication (if-conversion) versus prediction: when converting a hard-to-predict branch into predicated instructions wins, and what it costs.

Jiménez & Lin, Dynamic Branch Prediction with Perceptrons, HPCA 2001
Wisconsin CA qualifier, Fall 2020, Q2 (dealing with branches)

units.title: Cache coherence: snooping and directories
objectives: State the coherence invariants (single-writer–multiple-reader and data-value) and why private caches need coherence.
Trace MSI and MESI state transitions for a sequence of loads and stores from two cores, and say what the E and O states add (MESI, MOESI).
Contrast snooping (broadcast) with directory protocols (full-map, limited-pointer, sparse directories) by traffic, latency, storage and power.
Explain false sharing and compute its coherence traffic for an example.
Argue whether a low-power many-core design should drop hardware coherence.
refs: Nagarajan, Sorin, Hill & Wood, A Primer on Memory Consistency and Cache Coherence, 2nd ed., coherence chapters (snooping and directory protocols)
Wisconsin CA qualifier, Fall 2020, Q4 (cache coherence and power)

units.title: Memory consistency: SC, TSO and relaxed models
objectives: Define sequential consistency (Lamport, 1979) and explain why store buffers break it.
Work litmus tests (store buffering, message passing) and say which outcomes SC, x86-TSO and the Arm/RISC-V relaxed models allow.
Insert the minimal fences that make a message-passing idiom correct on a relaxed model.
State the DRF-SC guarantee: programs free of data races appear sequentially consistent.
refs: Nagarajan, Sorin, Hill & Wood, A Primer on Memory Consistency and Cache Coherence, 2nd ed., consistency chapters (SC, TSO, relaxed models)
Lamport, How to Make a Multiprocessor Computer That Correctly Executes Multiprocess Programs, IEEE Transactions on Computers C-28(9), 1979
Adve & Gharachorloo, Shared Memory Consistency Models: A Tutorial, IEEE Computer 29(12), 1996

units.title: Transactional memory and speculative lock elision
objectives: Explain hardware transactional memory: speculative execution of a critical section with conflict detection through the coherence protocol.
Explain speculative lock elision: run lock-protected code without taking the lock, commit if no conflict occurred, otherwise fall back to the lock.
Explain why best-effort HTM (as in Intel and IBM processors) is easier to build, and its pitfalls: capacity aborts, mandatory fallback paths, repeated aborts, hard debugging.
refs: Herlihy & Moss, Transactional Memory: Architectural Support for Lock-Free Data Structures, ISCA 1993
Rajwar & Goodman, Speculative Lock Elision, MICRO 2001
Wisconsin CA qualifier, Fall 2020, Q5 (speculative lock elision and transactional memory)

units.title: DRAM and memory controllers
objectives: Describe DRAM organization (channel, rank, bank, row, column) and the row buffer.
Compute access latency for a row hit, a row miss and a row conflict from tRCD, tCAS (CL) and tRP.
Compute peak bandwidth from bus width and transfer rate (e.g. 64 bits at 8533 MT/s ≈ 68 GB/s) and compare LPDDR, DDR and HBM.
Explain FR-FCFS scheduling and refresh overhead, and why DRAM energy per bit dwarfs on-chip SRAM.
refs: Jacob, Ng & Wang, Memory Systems: Cache, DRAM, Disk (2007)
Rixner et al., Memory Access Scheduling, ISCA 2000

units.title: Dark silicon and the limits of scaling
objectives: Explain Dennard scaling and why its end means not all transistors can switch at full speed at once (dark silicon).
Summarize Esmaeilzadeh et al.'s projection that multicore scaling alone cannot deliver historical speedups.

Name three SM features that give GPUs their throughput (many resident warps, SIMT execution, large register files and shared memory) and the scaling challenges that remain (power density, memory bandwidth).
refs: Esmaeilzadeh et al., Dark Silicon and the End of Multicore Scaling, ISCA 2011
Dennard et al., Design of Ion-Implanted MOSFETs with Very Small Physical Dimensions, IEEE JSSC 9(5), 1974

modules.title: Sparse accelerators
modules.summary: You will be able to design and evaluate hardware that skips work on zeros, from compressed formats to load balancing, and model it with Sparseloop.
refs: MIT 6.5930/1 (Spring 2026), L07 Sparsity and L08–L10 Sparse Architectures 1–3
Wu et al., Sparseloop: An Analytical Approach to Sparse Tensor Accelerator Modeling, MICRO 2022

practice.title: Timeloop and Sparseloop source

units.title: Sources of sparsity and compressed formats
objectives: Name the sources of zeros: ReLU activations, pruned weights, padding and sparse attention.
Encode a small matrix as a bitmask, run-length, COO, CSR and CSC and count the metadata bits of each.
Describe tensors as fibertrees (one level per rank, each stored uncompressed or compressed) as a general way to specify formats.
Compute the density below which a compressed format beats dense storage for given value and index widths.
refs: Kjolstad et al., The Tensor Algebra Compiler, OOPSLA 2017

units.title: Gating, skipping and intersection
objectives: Distinguish gating (detect a zero and idle the unit: saves energy, not time) from skipping (never schedule the work: saves time and energy).
Explain intersection of two compressed operand streams (two-finger merge) and leader–follower skipping.
Describe Cnvlutin (skips zero activations) and Eyeriss v2 (processes compressed weights and activations) as examples.
Correct the misconception that 50% sparsity yields a 2× speedup.
refs: Albericio et al., Cnvlutin: Ineffectual-Neuron-Free Deep Neural Network Computing, ISCA 2016
Chen et al., Eyeriss v2, IEEE JETCAS 2019

units.title: Landmark sparse accelerators: EIE and SCNN
objectives: Describe EIE: sparse fully connected layers stored in a CSC variant with relative indices and 4-bit shared-weight indices, with processing elements fed through activation queues.
Describe SCNN's Cartesian-product dataflow: multiply all nonzero weights by all nonzero activations in a PE and scatter products into an accumulator buffer.
Explain what each design exploits (weight sparsity, activation sparsity or both) and where its overheads arise (accumulator scatter, index logic).
refs: Han et al., EIE: Efficient Inference Engine on Compressed Deep Neural Network, ISCA 2016
Parashar et al., SCNN: An Accelerator for Compressed-sparse Convolutional Neural Networks, ISCA 2017

units.title: Structured sparsity: N:M and 2:4
objectives: Define N:M structured sparsity and explain why 2:4 (two nonzeros in every four) suits hardware: a fixed compression ratio and 2-bit position metadata per kept value.
Explain how Ampere sparse tensor cores and Arm Ethos-U85 use 2:4 to double math throughput, and the recipe (train dense → prune to 2:4 → retrain) that recovers accuracy.
Compute effective storage including metadata for 2:4 int8 weights (20 bits per group of four, 62.5% of dense).
Compare unstructured, block and N:M sparsity by accuracy, speedup and hardware cost.
refs: Mishra et al., Accelerating Sparse Deep Neural Networks, arXiv:2104.08378, 2021

units.title: Load balancing with irregular sparsity
objectives: Explain why uneven nonzero counts leave most PEs idle while one finishes.
Compare static balancing (reordering rows or columns, grouping by density) with dynamic balancing (work queues, work stealing).
Describe flexible interconnects (SIGMA) that map irregular sparse GEMMs onto PEs.
Correct the misconception that average density predicts run time.
refs: Qin et al., SIGMA: A Sparse and Irregular GEMM Accelerator with Flexible Interconnects for DNN Training, HPCA 2020

units.title: Modelling sparse accelerators with Sparseloop
objectives: Describe Sparseloop's decomposition of sparse acceleration features (representation format, gating, skipping) and per-tensor density models.
Use statistical density models to estimate energy and cycles saved, including metadata and intersection overheads.
Find the density at which a sparse design stops beating a dense one.

modules.title: Numerics co-design
modules.summary: You will be able to choose and justify number formats for ML hardware, from block floating point to OCP MX and NVFP4, including how accumulators, rounding and outliers affect accuracy.
refs: Rouhani et al., Microscaling Data Formats for Deep Learning, arXiv:2310.10537, 2023
Stanford CS217 (Winter 2026), Quantization lecture and HW2 (MXFP prologue vs epilogue cost)

practice.title: microxcaling: MX format emulation library (PyTorch)

units.title: The number-format design space
objectives: Explain how exponent bits buy range and mantissa bits buy precision, and compute the dynamic range of FP16, BF16, FP8 E4M3 and FP8 E5M2.
Compare OCP FP8 E4M3 (more precision, maximum 448) with E5M2 (more range, maximum 57,344) and say which suits weights and activations versus gradients.
Compare multiplier cost across INT8, FP8, BF16 and FP32.
Explain why integers are cheaper but need external scale factors, while floats carry a scale in every element.
refs: Micikevicius et al., FP8 Formats for Deep Learning, arXiv:2209.05433, 2022
OCP MX Specification v1.0, §5.3.1 (FP8 adopted from the OCP FP8 specification)

units.title: Block floating point
objectives: Define block floating point: k values share one exponent, so the dot product inside a block is integer arithmetic plus one exponent addition.
Compute the quantization error of a block containing one large outlier and explain why smaller blocks help.
Describe Microsoft Floating Point (MSFP) and shared microexponents as the steps that led to MX.
Trade block size against metadata bits and accuracy.
refs: Darvish Rouhani et al., Pushing the Limits of Narrow Precision Inferencing at Cloud Scale with Microsoft Floating Point, NeurIPS 2020
Rouhani et al., With Shared Microexponents, A Little Shifting Goes a Long Way, ISCA 2023
Drumond et al., Training DNNs with Hybrid Block Floating Point, NeurIPS 2018

units.title: OCP MX formats and NVFP4
objectives: State the MX structure (spec §5.1–5.2): k = 32 elements share one E8M0 power-of-two scale; the concrete formats are MXFP8 (E5M2 or E4M3), MXFP6 (E3M2 or E2M3), MXFP4 (E2M1) and MXINT8.
Compute bits per element: MXFP8 8.25, MXFP6 6.25, MXFP4 4.25 (4 + 8/32).

Apply the spec's conversion rule (§6.3): scale = largest power of two ≤ max|v| divided by the largest power of two of the element type, then round-to-nearest-even and clamp; and the dot product (§6.1) as the product of the two scales times the sum of element products.

Describe NVFP4 (NVIDIA, Jun 2025): 16-element blocks of E2M1 values with an FP8 E4M3 scale plus a per-tensor FP32 scale, about 4.5 bits per value, supported by Blackwell tensor cores; explain why a fractional scale and smaller blocks cut error compared with E8M0.
Place the landmark: OCP MX v1.0 (Sep 2023) from AMD, Arm, Intel, Meta, Microsoft, NVIDIA and Qualcomm.
refs: OCP Microscaling Formats (MX) Specification v1.0, §5.1–5.4 and §6.1–6.3
Rouhani et al., Microscaling Data Formats for Deep Learning, arXiv:2310.10537, 2023
Alvarez et al., Introducing NVFP4 for Efficient and Accurate Low-Precision Inference, NVIDIA Technical Blog, 24 Jun 2025

units.title: Accumulator width and overflow
objectives: Compute accumulator bit growth: a product of b_w-bit and b_a-bit integers needs b_w + b_a bits, and summing K products adds about ⌈log2 K⌉ more.
Explain why int8 × int8 uses int32 accumulators and int16 × int8 uses int48 in TOSA.
Explain accumulator-aware quantization (A2Q), which constrains weights so that a narrower accumulator provably cannot overflow.
Explain how FP16 versus FP32 accumulation inside tensor cores affects long dot products.
refs: Colbert et al., A2Q: Accumulator-Aware Quantization with Guaranteed Overflow Avoidance, ICCV 2023

units.title: Rounding and stochastic rounding
objectives: Compare round-to-nearest-even with stochastic rounding (round up with probability equal to the fractional distance to the next value).
Show that stochastic rounding is unbiased in expectation and why that matters when many tiny updates accumulate (swamping).
Explain Gupta et al.'s finding that 16-bit fixed-point training works with stochastic rounding but not with round-to-nearest.
Weigh the hardware cost (a random number per operation) against compensated (Kahan) summation and wider accumulators.
refs: Gupta et al., Deep Learning with Limited Numerical Precision, ICML 2015
Croci et al., Stochastic Rounding: Implementation, Error Analysis and Applications, Royal Society Open Science 9, 2022

units.title: Outliers and mixed precision
objectives: Explain emergent activation outliers in large transformers (a few channels far larger than the rest) and why per-tensor int8 fails on them.
Describe LLM.int8()'s mixed-precision decomposition: outlier feature dimensions in FP16, everything else in int8.
Contrast hardware responses: outlier-aware accelerators (OLAccel), precision-scalable units (Bit Fusion) and finer-grained scaling (per-channel, per-group, MX blocks).
Preview the software fixes taught in tier 8: smoothing and rotation.
refs: Dettmers et al., LLM.int8(): 8-bit Matrix Multiplication for Transformers at Scale, NeurIPS 2022
Park, Kim & Yoo, Energy-Efficient Neural Network Accelerator Based on Outlier-Aware Low-Precision Computation (OLAccel), ISCA 2018
Sharma et al., Bit Fusion, ISCA 2018

units.title: Pareto analysis
objectives: Define Pareto dominance and the Pareto front over objectives such as accuracy, latency, energy and area.
Compute the hypervolume of a 2-D front relative to a reference point to compare two sets of designs.
Contrast weighted-sum scalarization (misses non-convex parts of the front) with constraint-based search.
Spot misleading comparisons: different baselines, one point instead of a front, unreported accuracy.
refs: Janapa Reddi et al., mlsysbook.ai Vol. I, ch. 12 (Benchmarking)

units.title: Accelerator design-space exploration
objectives: List an accelerator's design parameters (array shape, buffer sizes, bandwidth, dataflow) and estimate the size of the design space.
Compare grid, random, Bayesian-optimization, reinforcement-learning and genetic search by the number of evaluations they need.
Run a DSE loop with a fast simulator (SCALE-Sim or Timeloop) in the loop and plot the resulting Pareto front.
Explain Interstellar's finding that loop blocking matters more than the choice of dataflow.

Kao, Jeong & Krishna, ConfuciuX: Autonomous Hardware Resource Assignment for DNN Accelerators using Reinforcement Learning, MICRO 2020
Georgia Tech ECE/CS 8803 HML (Spring 2025), Lab 2: Design-space exploration of an AI accelerator

units.title: Learned cost models
objectives: Explain why DSE and compilers use learned surrogates: each real measurement or detailed simulation is slow.
Describe a learned cost model's inputs (loop or graph features), training data (measured programs) and use (ranking candidates).
Explain transfer across hardware and the failure mode of distribution shift.
Describe surrogate-guided architecture exploration in the style of Apollo.

Yazdanbakhsh et al., Apollo: Transferable Architecture Exploration, arXiv:2102.01723, 2021

units.title: Joint search over networks and accelerators
objectives: Explain hardware-aware NAS: add measured or predicted latency to the search objective (FBNet, ProxylessNAS, Once-for-All).
Explain co-exploration: search network and accelerator parameters together, as NAAS does for accelerator sizing, connectivity, compiler mapping and the network.
Describe MCUNet's TinyNAS plus TinyEngine as system–algorithm co-design under MCU memory limits.
Weigh the cost of joint search against the gain over optimizing each side alone.
refs: Lin et al., NAAS: Neural Accelerator Architecture Search, DAC 2021
Cai et al., Once-for-All: Train One Network and Specialize it for Efficient Deployment, ICLR 2020

units.title: Scale-out parallelism and collectives
objectives: Define data, tensor (intra-layer) and pipeline parallelism and state what each must communicate.
Compute ring all-reduce time ≈ 2 (p − 1)/p × N ÷ B for N bytes, p devices and per-link bandwidth B.
Explain why topology-aware collectives and system simulators such as ASTRA-sim matter when co-designing multi-chip systems, including multi-die edge parts.
Explain overlapping communication with computation and why communication can dominate at scale.
refs: Janapa Reddi et al., mlsysbook.ai Vol. II, ch. 5 (Collective Communication) and ch. 6 (Distributed Training)
Rashidi et al., ASTRA-SIM: Enabling SW/HW Co-Design Exploration for Distributed DL Training Platforms, ISPASS 2020
Georgia Tech ECE/CS 8803 HML (Spring 2025), Labs 3–5 (distributed execution, ASTRA-sim DSE, TACOS collectives)

units.title: Co-design case studies
objectives: Explain TPU v4's co-design choices (optical circuit switches for a reconfigurable topology, SparseCores for embeddings) and what they show about designing for a workload.
Explain Eyeriss v2's flexible network-on-chip, designed for compact models such as MobileNet whose reuse varies by layer.
Summarize MCUNet's gains from designing the model and the inference engine together.
Draw the lesson: co-design pays when workloads are stable and well understood.

Chen et al., Eyeriss v2, IEEE JETCAS 2019

units.title: The memory cost of backpropagation
objectives: Break training memory into weights, gradients, optimizer state (Adam keeps two extra values per parameter) and saved activations.
Compute activation memory for a CNN at a given batch size and show that it exceeds parameter memory.
Explain gradient checkpointing (about √n memory for n layers at the cost of roughly one extra forward pass).
Explain why inference-time memory planning does not carry over directly to training.

units.title: Bias-only and other parameter-efficient updates
objectives: Explain TinyTL's insight: training memory is dominated by activations, not trainable parameters, so freezing weights and training only biases avoids storing most activations.
Show why the bias gradient does not need the layer's input activation while the weight gradient does.
Describe TinyTL's lite residual module (about 3.8% memory overhead) and its results: up to 6.5× less memory than full fine-tuning and up to 34.1% higher accuracy than last-layer-only fine-tuning.
Compare bias-only (BitFit), last-layer, LoRA and full fine-tuning by memory and accuracy.

Ben Zaken, Ravfogel & Goldberg, BitFit, ACL 2022

Explain Quantization-Aware Scaling: calibrate gradient scales so an int8 quantized graph without normalization trains stably.
Explain sparse update: choose which layers and sub-tensors to update by contribution analysis under a memory budget.
Weigh accuracy recovery against memory for full, bias-only and sparse-update schemes.

units.title: Training engines: compile-time autodiff and PockEngine
objectives: Explain why on-device training engines derive the backward graph at compile time instead of building it at run time.

Quote and qualify PockEngine's reported results: up to 15× faster than TensorFlow on Raspberry Pi, 5.6× back-propagation memory saving on Jetson AGX Orin, and LLaMA-2-7B fine-tuning at 550 tokens/s (7.9× faster than PyTorch).

Lin et al., On-Device Training Under 256KB Memory, NeurIPS 2022 (Tiny Training Engine)

units.title: Continual and personalized learning on device
objectives: Define catastrophic forgetting and compare replay buffers, regularization and parameter isolation as remedies within device memory limits.
Explain test-time adaptation, e.g. Tent: update only normalization parameters to minimize prediction entropy on incoming data.
Explain why labels are scarce on device and how self-supervision or user feedback supplies them.
Weigh the energy cost of on-device updates against cloud fine-tuning.

Explain non-IID data, stragglers and partial participation, and their effects on convergence.
Explain secure aggregation and differential privacy as protections, and what they cost.

units.title: Adversarial examples at the edge
objectives: Generate adversarial examples with FGSM (one step along the sign of the input gradient) and PGD (iterated, projected steps).
Explain physical-world attacks (patches, stickers) that matter for deployed cameras.
Explain how quantization can amplify adversarial noise and how defensive quantization (controlling the Lipschitz constant) helps.
Weigh adversarial training's cost against its robustness gain.

units.title: Fault injection and bit flips
objectives: Explain soft errors and why a flipped exponent bit in a floating-point weight does far more damage than a flipped low mantissa bit.
Describe the bit-flip attack (search for the few most damaging weight bits) and its delivery through Rowhammer (DeepHammer).
Describe voltage and clock glitching as physical fault-injection attacks on microcontrollers.
Compare defences: ECC, weight checksums, activation range restriction and redundancy.

units.title: Side channels and model extraction
objectives: Explain how timing, cache, power and electromagnetic side channels leak a model's architecture or weights (Cache Telepathy, CSI NN).
Explain model extraction through prediction queries and why on-device models are also exposed to physical probing.
Describe countermeasures: constant-time kernels, masking, noise injection and encrypted weights.

units.title: Trusted execution environments for ML
objectives: Describe Arm TrustZone for Cortex-A and Cortex-M: secure and non-secure worlds, secure boot and protected storage of model weights.
Explain partitioning a model so sensitive layers run inside the TEE (DarkneTZ) and verifiable offloading from an enclave (Slalom).
Weigh TEE protection against secure-memory limits and slowdown.
refs: Janapa Reddi et al., mlsysbook.ai Vol. II, ch. 13
Mo et al., DarkneTZ: Towards Model Privacy at the Edge using Trusted Execution Environments, MobiSys 2020

units.title: Privacy for on-device ML
objectives: Explain membership inference and why on-device processing alone does not guarantee privacy (updates and outputs still leak).
State the DP-SGD recipe: clip each example's gradient to norm C, add Gaussian noise, and track the privacy budget (ε, δ).
Compute how clipping norm and noise multiplier trade privacy against accuracy in a small example.
List the responsible-AI duties that remain on device: fairness testing across user groups, transparency about local data use, and safe update and rollback of deployed models.

Compute fleet energy as energy per inference × inferences per day × number of devices, and convert it to CO2e.
Use an ACT-style model to compare a larger, more efficient chip with a smaller chip that has less embodied carbon.

objectives: Rank analytical models, trace-driven simulation, cycle-level simulation, RTL simulation and FPGA-accelerated simulation (FireSim) by speed and fidelity.
Explain sampling methods (SimPoint phase-based, SMARTS statistical) that cut simulation time.
Choose a method for a question: a design-space sweep versus cycle-accurate validation.

units.title: gem5 in practice
objectives: Choose among gem5 CPU models (Atomic, Timing, Minor in-order, O3 out-of-order) and between syscall-emulation and full-system modes.
Write a Python configuration that builds a system with caches and runs a binary, then read stats.txt (simulated seconds, IPC, miss rates).
Avoid the pitfalls: no warm-up, measuring the whole program instead of the region of interest, mismatched ISA or configuration.

units.title: Chipyard and Gemmini
objectives: Describe Chipyard as an SoC generator framework (Rocket and BOOM cores, RoCC accelerators, flows from simulation to VLSI).
Configure Gemmini (systolic dimensions, weight- or output-stationary dataflow, scratchpad and accumulator sizes) and run a DNN through its software stack.
Explain Gemmini's full-system lesson: system effects such as virtual-address translation and host CPU speed change accelerator results.
Describe how Berkeley's EE 290-2 labs used FireSim to run ResNet-50 inference in minutes instead of hours of RTL simulation.

objectives: Compute dynamic power α·C·V²·f and explain leakage and why it grows at advanced nodes and high temperature.
Compare estimation levels: architectural (McPAT; Accelergy with CACTI), RTL or gate level with switching activity, and measurement.
Estimate a layer's energy from access counts and per-access energies, then compare with a measurement.
Follow a sound power-measurement method (sampling rate, idle subtraction, long enough runs), such as MLPerf's.

units.title: Statistical rigour in evaluation
objectives: Report variability with repetitions, confidence intervals and percentiles instead of a single run.
Use the geometric mean for normalized speedups and explain why the arithmetic mean of ratios misleads.
Explain measurement bias (environment size or link order changing results) and how randomizing setups exposes it.

units.title: Reading papers in three passes
objectives: Apply Keshav's first pass (5–10 minutes: title, abstract, introduction, section headings, conclusions, references) and answer the five Cs: category, context, correctness, contributions, clarity.
Apply the second pass (up to an hour: figures, graphs and key points, skipping proofs) and the third pass (virtually re-implement the paper to expose hidden assumptions).
Use the passes to survey the literature of a new subfield.

units.title: Venues and peer review

Explain double-blind review, rebuttals and conflicts of interest.

units.title: Landmark-paper timeline

units.title: The LLM quantization landscape
objectives: Classify schemes as weight-only (W4A16), weight-and-activation (W8A8, W4A4) and KV-cache quantization, using WxAyKVz notation.
Explain why 4-bit weight-only quantization speeds up batch-1 decode (memory-bound) but not compute-bound prefill.
Explain group-wise quantization (e.g. group size 128 or 32) and compute its scale overhead in bits per weight.
Explain why LLM activations, not weights, are the hard part: a few outlier channels.
refs: MIT 6.5940 (Fall 2026), L13 LLM Quantization and Deployment

units.title: GPTQ: second-order post-training quantization
objectives: State the layer-wise objective: choose quantized Ŵ to minimize ||WX − ŴX||² on calibration data, whose Hessian is H = 2XXᵀ.

Explain GPTQ's column-by-column quantization that compensates each column's error in the remaining columns (from Optimal Brain Quantization), with lazy batched updates and a Cholesky reformulation for numerical stability.
Quote the results: 175B-parameter models quantized in about 4 GPU hours to 3–4 bits with negligible accuracy loss; end-to-end speedups over FP16 of about 3.25× on A100 and 4.5× on A6000.
Explain why GPTQ needs calibration data and can overfit it.
refs: Frantar, Ashkboos, Hoefler & Alistarh, GPTQ: Accurate Post-Training Quantization for Generative Pre-trained Transformers, ICLR 2023 (arXiv:2210.17323)
Frantar & Alistarh, Optimal Brain Compression, NeurIPS 2022

units.title: AWQ: activation-aware weight quantization
objectives: Explain AWQ's observation: protecting about 1% of salient weight channels, identified by activation magnitude rather than weight magnitude, greatly reduces quantization error.
Show the equivalence y = (W·diag(s))(diag(s)⁻¹·x) and how scaling salient channels up before quantization protects them without mixed-precision storage.
Explain the per-channel scale search (a grid over an exponent of the average activation magnitude) and why using no backpropagation or reconstruction keeps AWQ from overfitting the calibration set.
Quote: the TinyChat runtime runs AWQ models more than 3× faster than the Hugging Face FP16 implementation on desktop and mobile GPUs; AWQ received the MLSys 2024 Best Paper Award.
refs: Lin et al., AWQ: Activation-aware Weight Quantization for LLM Compression and Acceleration, MLSys 2024 (arXiv:2306.00978)

units.title: SmoothQuant: W8A8 by smoothing
objectives: Explain migrating quantization difficulty from activations to weights with a per-channel smoothing factor s_j = max|X_j|^α ÷ max|W_j|^(1−α) (Eq. 4).
Pick the migration strength α (0.5 balances most models such as OPT and BLOOM; harder-to-quantize GLM-130B uses 0.75) and compute smoothed ranges for a toy example.
Explain why the smoothing factors fold offline into the preceding layer, so W8A8 runs for all matrix multiplies on int8 hardware.
Quote: up to 1.56× speedup and 2× memory reduction with negligible accuracy loss (ICML 2023).
refs: Xiao et al., SmoothQuant: Accurate and Efficient Post-Training Quantization for Large Language Models, ICML 2023 (arXiv:2211.10438), §4 and §5.1

units.title: QServe: W4A8KV4 system co-design
objectives: Explain why 4-bit schemes lose their benefit on GPUs in large-batch serving: dequantizing weights or partial sums on CUDA cores costs 20–90% runtime overhead.
Describe the QoQ algorithm: 4-bit weights with progressive (two-level) quantization so the GEMM main loop stays in int8, 8-bit activations, and a 4-bit KV cache made accurate by SmoothAttention.
Describe the system side: compute-aware weight reordering, register-level parallelism for dequantization and a fused memory-bound attention kernel.
Quote and qualify the throughput gains over TensorRT-LLM: 1.2× (A100) and 1.4× (L40S) on Llama-3-8B; 2.4× and 3.5× on Qwen1.5-72B (MLSys 2025).
refs: Lin et al., QServe: W4A8KV4 Quantization and System Co-design for Efficient LLM Serving, MLSys 2025 (arXiv:2405.04532)

units.title: Rotations: QuaRot and SpinQuant
objectives: Explain computational invariance: inserting an orthogonal matrix Q and its transpose around the residual stream leaves outputs unchanged while spreading outlier energy across channels.

Describe QuaRot: Hadamard rotations fused into the weights plus online Hadamard transforms, giving 4-bit weights, activations and KV cache with no channels kept at high precision; 4-bit LLaMA2-70B loses at most 0.47 WikiText-2 perplexity and keeps 99% of zero-shot accuracy (NeurIPS 2024).

Describe SpinQuant: learn rotations R1 and R2 with Cayley SGD on the Stiefel manifold while R3 and R4 stay Hadamard; with 4-bit weights, activations and KV cache the zero-shot gap to full precision is 2.9 points on LLaMA-2 7B, and up to 45.1% smaller than QuaRot's on LLaMA-3 8B (ICLR 2025).
Explain why Meta used SpinQuant (no training data needed) for one of its quantized Llama 3.2 1B/3B releases.
refs: Ashkboos et al., QuaRot: Outlier-Free 4-Bit Inference in Rotated LLMs, NeurIPS 2024 (arXiv:2404.00456)
Liu et al., SpinQuant: LLM Quantization with Learned Rotations, ICLR 2025 (arXiv:2405.16406), §3.2
Meta AI blog, quantized Llama 3.2 1B and 3B models, 24 Oct 2024

units.title: Ternary LLMs: BitNet b1.58
objectives: Explain BitNet b1.58: weights in {−1, 0, +1} via absmean quantization (log2 3 ≈ 1.58 bits), activations quantized to 8 bits per token with absmax, and training from scratch rather than quantizing after training.
Explain why ternary weights turn matrix multiply into additions and subtractions and what that implies for hardware.
Quote BitNet b1.58 2B4T (Apr 2025): 2B parameters, 4T training tokens, 0.4 GB non-embedding memory and 29 ms CPU decoding latency per token (authors' report).
Contrast native low-bit training with post-training ternarization and correct the misconception that any trained model can simply be ternarized.
refs: Ma et al., The Era of 1-bit LLMs: All Large Language Models are in 1.58 Bits, arXiv:2402.17764, 2024
Ma et al., BitNet b1.58 2B4T Technical Report, arXiv:2504.12285, 2025, §2

units.title: Prefill, decode and the memory wall
objectives: Explain prefill (the prompt processed in parallel: matrix–matrix, compute-bound) versus decode (one token at a time: matrix–vector, memory-bound), with the metrics time to first token and time per output token.
Estimate the decode ceiling: tokens/s ≲ memory bandwidth ÷ weight bytes read per token, e.g. a 3B model at 4 bits (≈1.5 GB) on 60 GB/s LPDDR gives at most about 40 tokens/s.
Compute KV-cache bytes = 2 × layers × KV heads × head dimension × sequence length × bytes per element, and show how grouped-query attention reduces it.
Explain why batching raises decode throughput on servers but rarely helps a single-user device.
refs: Pope et al., Efficiently Scaling Transformer Inference, MLSys 2023
Ainslie et al., GQA: Training Generalized Multi-Query Transformer Models from Multi-Head Checkpoints, EMNLP 2023

units.title: KV-cache management
objectives: Explain PagedAttention: store the KV cache in fixed-size blocks indexed by a block table, like virtual-memory pages, to avoid fragmentation and allow sharing (SOSP 2023; 2–4× serving throughput over prior systems).
Compute savings from 8-bit or 4-bit KV-cache quantization and from cross-layer KV sharing (Apple's on-device model reuses block 1's KV cache in block 2, cutting KV memory by 37.5%).
Explain prompt caching, sliding-window attention and attention sinks (StreamingLLM keeps the first few tokens plus a recent window) as ways to bound KV memory on device.
Weigh context length against device memory.
refs: Kwon et al., Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention, SOSP 2023 (arXiv:2309.06180)
Apple, Apple Intelligence Foundation Language Models Tech Report 2025 (arXiv:2507.13575), §2.1
Xiao et al., Efficient Streaming Language Models with Attention Sinks, ICLR 2024 (arXiv:2309.17453)

units.title: FlashAttention and IO-aware attention on device
objectives: Explain FlashAttention's tiling of Q, K and V through on-chip memory with an online softmax so the N × N score matrix never reaches off-chip memory, and why the result is exact, not approximate.
Compute off-chip traffic for naive attention versus FlashAttention for a given sequence length and head dimension.

Describe FlashAttention-2's improved work partitioning (about 2× faster than FlashAttention, 50–73% of A100 peak FLOPs) and how splitting the KV sequence across parallel workers adapts the idea to single-token decode.
Judge when IO-aware attention matters on mobile GPUs and NPUs (long prompts) and when it does not (short-context decode).
refs: Dao et al., FlashAttention: Fast and Memory-Efficient Exact Attention with IO-Awareness, NeurIPS 2022
Dao, FlashAttention-2: Faster Attention with Better Parallelism and Work Partitioning, arXiv:2307.08691, 2023

units.title: Speculative decoding
objectives: Explain draft-and-verify: a cheap draft model proposes γ tokens and the target model checks them all in one parallel pass.

State the acceptance rule (keep a drafted token x with probability min(1, p(x) / q(x)), otherwise resample from the normalized residual) and why it reproduces the target distribution exactly (Leviathan et al., §2.3).
Compute expected tokens per target pass, (1 − α^(γ+1)) ÷ (1 − α), for acceptance rate α (§3.1), and the resulting speedup given the draft's cost.

Weigh a draft model's memory on device against its speedup, describe self-drafting with nested sub-models (MatFormer), and note that MLPerf Inference v6.1 (Sep 2026) allows speculative decoding in its interactive scenario.
refs: Leviathan, Kalman & Matias, Fast Inference from Transformers via Speculative Decoding, ICML 2023 (arXiv:2211.17192), §2.3 and §3.1
Chen et al., Accelerating Large Language Model Decoding with Speculative Sampling, arXiv:2302.01318, 2023
MLCommons, MLPerf Inference v6.1 results announcement, 16 Sep 2026

units.title: llama.cpp and GGUF
objectives: Describe llama.cpp: a C/C++ LLM runtime built on the ggml tensor library, with SIMD CPU kernels and Metal, CUDA and Vulkan backends.
Describe a GGUF file: the 'GGUF' magic, version 3, typed key–value metadata, a tensor-info table and tensor data aligned (default 32 bytes) for memory-mapped loading.
Compare quantization types: legacy Q4_0 and Q8_0, K-quants (Q2_K to Q6_K), IQ types, ternary TQ1_0/TQ2_0 and the newer MXFP4 and NVFP4 entries.
Benchmark a model with llama-bench and report prompt-processing (prefill) and generation (decode) tokens/s separately.

units.title: MLC LLM, ExecuTorch and LiteRT-LM
objectives: Describe MLC LLM: compile with Apache TVM (gen_config → convert_weight → compile) and serve through MLCEngine's OpenAI-style API on CUDA, Vulkan, Metal, iOS, Android and in browsers through WebGPU (WebLLM).

Describe ExecuTorch 1.0 (general availability, Oct 2025): PyTorch-native export to .pte; production-ready XNNPACK (with Arm KleidiAI), Core ML, Qualcomm AI Engine, Arm Ethos-U and Vulkan backends; LLM and multimodal export, e.g. through Hugging Face optimum-executorch.

Describe LiteRT-LM: Google's open-source LLM framework layered on LiteRT (formerly TensorFlow Lite), with .litertlm bundles, GPU and NPU acceleration, and Android, iOS, web, desktop and IoT targets; it powers on-device GenAI in Chrome, Chromebook Plus and Pixel Watch.
Choose among these and llama.cpp for a target device by backend coverage, model coverage and integration effort.
refs: PyTorch, Introducing ExecuTorch 1.0, PyTorch blog, Oct 2025
Google AI Edge Team, TensorFlow Lite is now LiteRT, Google Developers Blog, 4 Sep 2024

units.title: bitnet.cpp and lookup-table kernels
objectives: Describe bitnet.cpp (v1.0, Oct 2024): Microsoft's inference framework for 1.58-bit models, with the I2_S kernel (2-bit packed weights) and lookup-table kernels TL1 (Arm) and TL2 (x86), plus a GPU kernel added in May 2025.
Explain the lookup-table idea: precompute partial sums of activations for every pattern of a small group of ternary weights, then replace multiply–adds with table lookups.
Quote and qualify the reported CPU results: 1.37–5.07× speedup with 55.4–70.0% less energy on Arm, 2.37–6.17× with 71.9–82.2% less on x86, and a 100B ternary model at about 5–7 tokens/s on one CPU.
refs: Wang et al., 1-bit AI Infra: Part 1.1, Fast and Lossless BitNet b1.58 Inference on CPUs, arXiv:2410.16144, 2024
Wang et al., Bitnet.cpp: Efficient Edge Inference for Ternary LLMs, arXiv:2502.11880, 2025

units.title: Llama 3.2 1B and 3B
objectives: Describe how Llama 3.2 1B and 3B (Sep 2024) were made: one-shot structured pruning from Llama 3.1 8B, then knowledge distillation using logits from Llama 3.1 8B and 70B; text-only, 128K-token context.

Describe the quantized release (Oct 2024): QAT with LoRA adaptors (QLoRA) for accuracy and SpinQuant for portability; 4-bit group-wise weights (group size 32) with 8-bit per-token dynamic activations in transformer blocks; 8-bit per-channel embeddings and classifier weights.
Quote Meta's measurements on a OnePlus 12 (vendor-reported): 2–4× speedup, decode 2.5× and prefill 4.2× faster, 56% smaller and 41% less memory than BF16, running on ExecuTorch with KleidiAI kernels.
Compute the weight memory of the 1B and 3B models in BF16 and in the 4-bit scheme.

units.title: Gemma 3n: MatFormer and per-layer embeddings
objectives: Explain MatFormer: nested feed-forward blocks trained jointly so smaller models are sub-networks of a larger one (NeurIPS 2024); Gemma 3n trains an E2B model inside E4B, and Mix-n-Match builds in-between sizes by choosing per-layer FFN widths (8192 to 16384) and skipping layers.

Explain Per-Layer Embeddings: per-layer embedding parameters are handled on the CPU so only about 2B (E2B) or 4B (E4B) core parameters must sit in accelerator memory; raw parameter counts are 5B and 8B, running in as little as 2 GB and 3 GB.

Describe Gemma 3n's KV-cache sharing (middle-layer keys and values reused by top layers during prefill, about 2× faster prefill than Gemma 3 4B), the MobileNet-V5 vision encoder and the USM-based audio encoder (one token per 160 ms).
Note the successor: Gemma 4 (2 Apr 2026) keeps edge E2B and E4B models with native audio input and a 128K context window.

Devvrit et al., MatFormer: Nested Transformer for Elastic Inference, NeurIPS 2024 (arXiv:2310.07707)
Google, Gemma 4: Byte for byte, the most capable open models, The Keyword, 2 Apr 2026

units.title: Apple's ~3B on-device foundation model
objectives: Describe the architecture split (§2.1): block 1 holds 62.5% of the transformer layers; block 2 (37.5%) has no key and value projections and reuses block 1's KV cache, cutting KV-cache memory by 37.5% and time to first token by about 37.5%.

Describe compression (§6): the ~3B on-device model's weights are compressed to 2 bits per weight with quantization-aware training, embeddings to 4 bits and the KV cache to 8 bits; the server PT-MoE model is compressed to 3.56 bits per weight with ASTC.
Explain the LoRA quality-recovery adapters and quote the cost: on-device MMLU falls from 67.8 to 64.4 after compression (§8, Table 3).
Compute the weight footprint of a 3B model at 2, 4 and 16 bits per weight.

Apple Machine Learning Research, Apple Intelligence Foundation Language Models Tech Report 2025, Jul 2025

Compute the share of parameters held in embeddings for a small model with a large vocabulary and explain why it matters at 1–3B scale.
Correct the misconception that parameter count alone predicts on-device speed: bits per weight, KV-cache size and memory placement matter as much.
Explain how swappable adapters let one base model serve many tasks or users on a device.

units.title: Efficient ViTs and linear attention
objectives: Compute how ViT attention cost grows with image resolution: tokens grow with pixel count and softmax attention with the square of the tokens.
Explain EfficientViT's multi-scale linear attention: ReLU linear attention computes Q(KᵀV) instead of (QKᵀ)V, linear in token count, using only hardware-friendly operators.
Quote EfficientViT's reported results (ICCV 2023): up to 13.9× lower GPU latency than SegFormer on Cityscapes and 48.9× higher throughput for Segment Anything on an A100.

units.title: Token merging
objectives: Explain ToMe's bipartite soft matching: split tokens into two sets, match each token to its most similar partner, and merge the r most similar pairs in every block, between the attention and MLP branches (§3).
Compute the tokens remaining after L blocks with r merged per block, and the resulting throughput gain.
Quote: training-free 2× throughput for ViT-L@512 and ViT-H@518 with a 0.2–0.3% accuracy drop (ICLR 2023 oral), and compare merging with pruning tokens.

units.title: Few-step diffusion
objectives: Explain why diffusion sampling is slow (tens of denoising-network evaluations per image) and the main step-reduction families: progressive distillation, consistency models, latent consistency models (2–4 steps; a 768 × 768 LCM distils in 32 A100 GPU-hours) and adversarial diffusion distillation (SDXL Turbo).
Correct the misconception that fewer steps are free: quality, diversity and guidance trade-offs.
Estimate on-device latency as steps × per-step network latency + decoder time, and compare a 25-step and a 4-step pipeline.

units.title: SVDQuant: 4-bit diffusion models
objectives: Explain why smoothing alone fails at 4-bit weights and activations for diffusion models, and SVDQuant's fix: move activation outliers into the weights, absorb them with a high-precision low-rank branch from an SVD, and quantize the residual to 4 bits.
Explain how the Nunchaku engine fuses the low-rank branch's kernels into the 4-bit kernels to avoid extra memory traffic, and keeps existing LoRA adapters working without re-quantization.
Quote (ICLR 2025 spotlight): on the 12B FLUX.1 models, 3.5× less memory and a 3.0× speedup over the W4A16 baseline on a 16 GB laptop RTX 4090 (INT4), and 3.1× on an RTX 5090 with NVFP4.
